The earth, like a mother giving birth, brings forth its full strength. Truth springs up from it, heaven smiles upon it, and it is clothed in God’s glory because he dwells with his people.

f.g: Labored in childbirth.

f.w: truth is established in her bowels

chapters.n: The song ends in praise: glory, honor, power, and might belong to God, who is full of mercy, justice, grace, truth, and peace forever.
Practical instructions begin. Missionaries with families who receive money as gifts should send it home or use it for their families, as the Lord directs.
Those without families should send money they receive to the bishop in Zion or Ohio to fund printing the revelations and building Zion.

f.g: The revelations were being prepared for publication as the Book of Commandments.

chapters.n: If someone gives them a new coat or suit, they should give the old one to the poor and go on their way happily.
Those strong in the Spirit should take along someone weaker so that person can grow strong too, with humility on both sides.

f.g: Built up, strengthened spiritually.

chapters.n: Elders should take Aaronic Priesthood holders with them to set up meetings, prepare the way, and fill appointments the elders can’t reach.

f.g: Arrange preaching meetings.

chapters.n: This is how the ancient apostles built up the Church.
Each person should serve in his own role. Using Paul’s image, the body needs its feet as much as its head.

f.w: let not the head say unto the feet

chapters.n: Every member is needed so all can be built up together and the whole “system” stays healthy and complete.

f.w: the body hath need of every member

chapters.n: High priests, elders, and priests should travel and preach, while teachers and deacons serve as “standing ministers” to watch over local congregations.
Bishop Newel K. Whitney is to travel among the branches looking for the poor and caring for them, humbling the rich and proud in the process.

f.g: A Kirtland merchant called as bishop in December 1831.

chapters.n: He should hire an agent to handle his business affairs as he directs.

f.g: Worldly, everyday (as opposed to religious).

chapters.n: Bishop Whitney is also to warn New York City, Albany, and Boston that they face desolation if they reject the gospel. He and Joseph Smith traveled east that fall.
If those cities reject the message, their judgment is near and their house will be left empty—words Jesus spoke over Jerusalem.

f.w: their house shall be left unto them desolate

chapters.n: If he trusts the Lord he won’t be put to shame, and God will watch over him in every detail.

f.g: Put to shame, defeated.

chapters.n: The other elders should go as their circumstances allow to the major cities and towns, clearly explaining the “desolation of abomination” coming in the last days.
The Lord will tear down worldly kingdoms. Not only the earth but even the starry heavens will tremble.
Though they can’t see it yet, the Lord has already set heaven’s powers in motion. Soon they will see it and know he will come to reign with his people.
The revelation closes with Christ as Alpha and Omega—the one who frames all of history.

Taken from a letter Joseph Smith wrote to W. W. Phelps in Missouri. The Lord’s appointed clerk (John Whitmer at the time) must keep a history and record of Zion, including who consecrated property and received inheritances from the bishop.
The record should also note how people live, their faith and works, and anyone who falls away after receiving an inheritance.

f.g: Abandon the faith one once accepted.

chapters.n: Those who did not receive their land through consecration, as the Lord’s law required, should not be listed among God’s people in Zion. This law was meant to prepare the Saints for the coming day of judgment.

f.w: that he may tithe his people
f.g: Here “tithe” refers broadly to the consecrated offerings of the law of the Lord.

f.w: the day of vengeance and burning

chapters.n: Their family records were not to be kept in the Church’s records either.

f.g: Family records showing descent.

chapters.n: Neither they nor their parents nor children will appear in “the book of the law of God”—the record of those who live the covenant.

f.w: the book of the law of God

f.g: Lord of armies—God as commander of heaven’s forces.

chapters.n: Joseph describes how revelation came: a still, small voice that whispers yet penetrates everything, sometimes making his very bones tremble.

The Lord will send “one mighty and strong” to set his house in order and assign inheritances. Church leaders in 1905 explained this prophecy was tied to the specific situation in Zion at the time and has often been misused by people claiming to be this figure.

f.g: A rod held by a ruler as a symbol of authority.
In old English, the inner self—the seat of feelings.

chapters.n: A warning drawn from Uzzah, who reached out to steady the ark and was struck down. Many understand it as a caution to Bishop Edward Partridge, who was then at odds with Joseph Smith; he later repented, and the warning did not fall on him.

f.g: To presume to correct the Lord’s work or his chosen leaders beyond one’s calling.
Arrow or bolt.

chapters.n: Those not written in the book of remembrance will have no inheritance in that day; they will be cut off and placed among unbelievers, where there is deep sorrow.

f.g: Grinding one’s teeth in anguish.

chapters.n: Joseph insists these words are not his own; what the Lord says, he will fulfill.
Priesthood holders and members who are not recorded, who have apostatized, or who have been cut off will not receive an inheritance among the Saints in that day.
They will be treated like the priests’ families in Ezra’s day who couldn’t find their genealogy and were excluded from the priesthood. Faithful record-keeping mattered then and now.

f.w: the second chapter and sixty-first and second verses of Ezra

chapters.n: While revising the Bible, Joseph Smith received this explanation of Jesus’s parable of the wheat and the tares, applying it to Church history and the last days.

f.w: the parable of the wheat and of the tares

chapters.n: The field is the world, and the sowers of the good seed were Christ’s ancient apostles, who planted the gospel and the Church.

After the apostles died, the great apostate power—called Babylon or the whore—sowed weeds among the wheat. Satan reigned in its heart, and the true Church was driven into the wilderness (the Great Apostasy).

f.g: A weed (probably darnel) that looks like wheat while young.

f.w: drive the church into the wilderness

chapters.n: Now in the last days, as the Lord restores his word, the young plant of the Church is just sprouting and still tender.

f.g: The first green shoot of a grain plant.

chapters.n: Angels are pleading with the Lord day and night, ready to go out and reap the harvest in judgment.
But the Lord tells them not to uproot the weeds yet, because the Saints’ faith is still weak and the good wheat would be destroyed too.
Wheat and tares grow together until harvest. Then—reversing the order in Matthew—the wheat (the righteous) is gathered first; afterward the tares are bundled and the field is burned.

f.g: In Matthew 13:30 the tares are gathered first; here the righteous are gathered out before the burning.

f.w: the field remaineth to be burned

chapters.n: The Lord now addresses those through whose family lines the priesthood has come down.
They are rightful heirs by birth, descended from Israel, whose identity was hidden from the world but known to God.

f.w: hid from the world with Christ in God

chapters.n: Their lives and priesthood were preserved and must continue through their descendants until the restoration of all things the prophets foretold.
They are blessed if they remain faithful: a light to the Gentiles and, through the priesthood, saviors to scattered Israel.

Given on Christmas Day 1832, during the “nullification crisis,” when South Carolina defied federal law. The Lord foretells wars beginning with a South Carolina rebellion. The Civil War began there at Fort Sumter in April 1861, more than 28 years later.

f.g: South Carolina was the first state to secede (December 1860), and the Civil War’s first shots were fired at Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor.

chapters.n: From that beginning, war would eventually spread to all nations.

f.w: war will be poured out upon all nations

chapters.n: The South would divide from the North and seek help from other nations, including Great Britain—which the Confederacy did attempt. Nations would then call on other nations, widening war worldwide.

f.g: The Confederacy sought British recognition and support during the Civil War.

chapters.n: Enslaved people would rise against their masters and be organized and trained for war. During the Civil War, many formerly enslaved men fought as soldiers.

f.g: Organized into military ranks.

chapters.n: The “remnants” left in the land—understood by Latter-day Saints as the descendants of Book of Mormon peoples—would rise up and greatly trouble the Gentiles.

f.g: Trouble, distress.

chapters.n: Through war, famine, plague, earthquake, and storms, people everywhere will feel God’s chastening, until the decreed end comes to all nations as they now exist.

f.g: The complete ending that God has determined.

f.w: a full end of all nations

chapters.n: This will happen so that the cries of persecuted Saints and their shed blood no longer rise to the Lord asking for justice.

f.g: Hebrew for “Lord of Hosts”—Lord of armies.

chapters.n: The response for the Saints is not panic but faithfulness: stand in holy places and don’t be moved, for the Lord’s coming is near.

Joseph Smith and other high priests gathered in Kirtland to pray to know the Lord’s will about building Zion. Joseph called this revelation “the olive leaf … plucked from the Tree of Paradise,” a message of peace from God.

f.g: A conference of high priests met in the translating room of Newel K. Whitney’s store in December 1832.

chapters.n: The Lord is pleased. Angels rejoice, and their prayers—offered like gifts—have reached him and are recorded among the names of the sanctified in the celestial world.

f.g: Prayers pictured as offerings given to God.
Lord of Hosts (armies).

f.w: book of the names of the sanctified

chapters.n: Christ sends “another Comforter”—here the Holy Spirit of promise—to dwell in their hearts, the same one he promised his disciples in John’s Gospel.

f.g: The Holy Ghost acting to seal and confirm covenants and blessings.

chapters.n: This Comforter is God’s promise of eternal life—the glory of the celestial kingdom.
That glory is shared by the Church of the Firstborn—those exalted through Jesus Christ, God’s Son.
Christ ascended above all after first descending below all, so he understands everything. He is in and through all things as the light of truth.
That truth shines: it is the Light of Christ. He is in the sun, its light, and the power by which the sun was made.
He is also the light and the creative power of the moon.
And of the stars and the power that made them.
And of the earth we stand on—his power holds it together.
The light that lets us see is the same light that “quickens” (enlivens) our minds and understanding. Physical light and spiritual insight come from the same source.

f.g: Gives life to; awakens.

chapters.n: This light goes out from God’s presence to fill the vastness of space.
It is in everything, gives life to everything, and is the law that governs all things—God’s own power, flowing from his throne at the center of eternity.

f.w: the law by which all things are governed

chapters.n: Christ’s redemption brings about resurrection from the dead.
A key Latter-day Saint teaching: the “soul” is the spirit and body together, not the spirit alone.
So resurrection—reuniting spirit and body forever—is the redemption of the whole soul.
That redemption comes through Christ, who gives life to all things and has decreed that the poor and meek will inherit the earth.

f.w: the meek of the earth shall inherit it

chapters.n: So the earth itself must be cleansed of all unrighteousness to prepare it for celestial glory.

f.g: Made holy, cleansed, set apart for God.

chapters.n: After the earth fulfills its purpose, it will be crowned with glory—even the presence of God the Father.

f.w: filled the measure of its creation
f.g: Fulfilled the purpose for which it was made.

chapters.n: Celestial beings, with resurrected bodies, will live on this glorified earth forever. That was the purpose of its creation.

f.w: for this intent was it made

chapters.n: Those who are not sanctified by the law of Christ will inherit a lesser kingdom—terrestrial or telestial.
We can only dwell in a glory whose laws we are able to live. Heaven is a fit, not just a reward.

f.g: Endure, live by, remain in.

chapters.n: The same is true of the terrestrial glory.
And of the telestial; those who can’t live even that law are not fit for any kingdom of glory and must remain in a kingdom without glory.

f.g: Fit, suitable.

f.w: a kingdom which is not a kingdom of glory

chapters.n: The earth itself obeys a celestial law—it fulfills its purpose and does not break God’s law.
So it will be sanctified. Though it will “die,” it will be brought back to life and the righteous will inherit it.
Likewise the righteous, though they die, will rise with a spiritual (resurrected, immortal) body.
Those with celestial spirits will receive the same body they had in mortality, now glorified with the glory that raises it.

f.w: the same body which was a natural body

chapters.n: Those who received a portion of celestial glory in this life will receive its fulness in the resurrection.
The same principle applies for terrestrial glory.
And for telestial glory. What we become here shapes what we receive there.
Even the rest will be resurrected, but will go to their own place, enjoying only what they were willing to receive.
What good is a gift a person won’t accept? They neither enjoy it nor love the giver. God’s greatest gifts must be received.

f.w: if a gift is bestowed upon him

chapters.n: Whatever lives by law is protected, perfected, and made holy by that law.
But whoever breaks law, tries to be a law to himself, and chooses to stay in sin cannot be sanctified by law, mercy, justice, or judgment. He remains unclean.
Every kingdom has its own law.
There are many kingdoms filling all space, greater and lesser—a vast view of God’s creations.

f.w: there is no space in the which there is no kingdom

chapters.n: Each kingdom has a law, and each law has limits and conditions.

f.g: Limits, boundaries.

chapters.n: Those who don’t live within those conditions are not justified (approved by God).

f.g: Declared right before God; pardoned.

chapters.n: Like attracts like: intelligence clings to intelligence, truth to truth, light to light. Mercy claims its own, justice claims its own, and judgment goes before God’s throne.
God understands everything; all things are before him, around him, in and through him. Everything exists by and from him forever.
He has given a law to all things, by which they move in their proper times and seasons.
Their paths are fixed—the courses of the heavens, the earth, and all the planets.
They give light to each other through minutes, hours, days, and years—yet all of it is like “one year” to God. His time is not ours.
A poetic picture: the earth and stars “roll upon their wings” in glory, held in God’s power, as sun and moon give their light.

f.g: A poetic image of the earth’s motion through space.

chapters.n: The Lord asks what he can compare these kingdoms to so his people can understand.
Anyone who has seen even the least of these creations has seen God moving in his majesty and power.
They have truly seen him in his works; yet when he came to his own people, they did not understand him.

f.w: he who came unto his own

chapters.n: The light shines in darkness and the darkness doesn’t grasp it. But the day will come when they will comprehend God himself, made alive in him.
Then they will know they have seen Christ—that he is the true light within them and they are in him. Without him they could not grow.

f.g: Grow, flourish, increase.

chapters.n: A parable: a man sends servants into his field to dig.
He tells the first that he will come in the first hour, and the servant will see the joy on his face.

f.g: Face, expression.

chapters.n: He tells the second he will visit in the second hour.
And the third likewise.
And so on through all twelve servants.
The lord comes to the first servant in the first hour and stays the full hour; the servant is filled with joy in his master’s presence.
Then he leaves to visit the second, third, and so on through the twelfth.
Each servant receives his lord’s presence in his own hour and season.

f.w: in his time, and in his season

chapters.n: The visits go from first to last and back again in turn—no one is neglected.
Each serves in his own order until his hour ends, so that the lord is glorified in each servant and each in the lord—and all are glorified together.

f.w: that his lord might be glorified in him

chapters.n: So it is with God’s many kingdoms and their inhabitants: each receives God’s presence in its own time, according to his decree.
The Lord leaves these teachings for them to ponder, and commands them to call on him while he is near.

f.w: call upon me while I am near

chapters.n: Draw near to him and he will draw near to you; seek, ask, and knock, and he will answer.

f.w: Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you

chapters.n: Whatever they ask the Father in Christ’s name will be given—if it is good for them.

f.g: Useful, wise, beneficial.

chapters.n: Asking for what isn’t good for us can bring condemnation. Prayer is aligning our will with God’s, not overriding it.
Christ’s voice is like a voice crying in the wilderness—they can’t see him—but his voice is Spirit, his Spirit is truth, and truth endures forever and grows within those who have it.

f.w: the voice of one crying in the wilderness
truth abideth and hath no end

chapters.n: If their focus is single to Christ’s glory, their whole body will be filled with light, and such a body comprehends all things.
So they should sanctify themselves and focus their minds on God. The time will come when he will unveil his face to them—in his own time, way, and will.

f.w: he will unveil his face unto you

chapters.n: Remember his great and last promise—to see his face. Put away idle thoughts and excessive, shallow laughter.

f.g: Not a ban on humor, but on frivolity that crowds out reverence.

chapters.n: They are to stay in Kirtland and call a solemn assembly of the first laborers in this final dispensation.

f.g: A sacred gathering for special instruction and worship.
Stay, remain.

chapters.n: Meanwhile those they warned on their missions should pray and ponder that warning for a while.

f.g: A short time.

chapters.n: The Lord will care for the members they taught and send other elders to them.

f.w: I will take care of your flocks

chapters.n: He will speed up his work when the time is right.

f.w: hasten my work in its time

chapters.n: The first laborers must gather, organize, prepare, and sanctify themselves—purifying hearts and cleansing hands and feet so the Lord can make them clean.

f.w: cleanse your hands and your feet

chapters.n: Then Christ can testify to the Father that they are clean from the sins of their generation and fulfill his great promise in his own time.

f.w: clean from the blood of this wicked generation

chapters.n: They are to continue in prayer and fasting from now on.
And they must teach one another the doctrines of the kingdom.
As they teach diligently, God’s grace will help them learn theory, principle, doctrine, and all the gospel requires.
Their learning should be broad: heaven and earth, past, present, and future, local and world affairs, wars and nations, and geography.

f.w: knowledge also of countries and of kingdoms

chapters.n: All of this is to prepare them for their missions when the Lord sends them again.
Those who have been warned have a duty to warn their neighbors.
So people are left without excuse, and responsibility for their sins rests on themselves.

f.w: their sins are upon their own heads

chapters.n: Whoever seeks the Lord early will find him and not be abandoned.
They should stay and work hard to be prepared to go to the Gentiles a final time, to “bind up the law and seal up the testimony” and prepare the Saints for judgment.

f.w: bind up the law and seal up the testimony
f.g: To complete the witness so that it stands as evidence for judgment.

chapters.n: This is so souls can escape God’s wrath. Elders not among the first laborers should keep working until called; their garments aren’t yet clean of this generation’s blood.

f.g: A common scriptural symbol for the Lord’s field of labor.

chapters.n: Stay in the freedom Christ gives; don’t get tangled in sin; keep your hands clean until he comes.

f.w: the liberty wherewith ye are made free

chapters.n: Soon the earth will stagger like a drunkard, the sun will darken, the moon will be red as blood, and stars will fall like figs shaken from a tree.

f.w: reel to and fro as a drunken man
the moon shall be bathed in blood

chapters.n: After the missionaries’ testimony comes God’s wrath and indignation.
Then comes the “testimony” of earthquakes, so severe that people fall to the ground.
Also the “voice” of thunder, lightning, storms, and seas surging beyond their bounds—nature itself testifying.

f.w: the waves of the sea heaving themselves beyond their bounds

chapters.n: Everything will be in turmoil; people’s hearts will fail from fear.
Angels will cry out with trumpets: prepare, for judgment has come; the Bridegroom is coming—go out to meet him.

f.g: Trumpet.

chapters.n: Then a great sign will appear in heaven that everyone will see at once.
Another angel will announce that the great and abominable church—which led nations into wickedness and persecuted the Saints—is the tares, bound and ready to be burned.

f.w: she is the tares of the earth

chapters.n: Heaven will be silent for half an hour; then the curtain of heaven will be unrolled like a scroll, and the Lord’s face revealed.

f.w: silence in heaven for the space of half an hour

chapters.n: Righteous Saints still alive will be changed and caught up to meet him.
The righteous dead will rise from their graves and be caught up too.
These are Christ’s “first fruits”—those raised in the first resurrection, who will descend with him.
A second trumpet: the redemption of those who are Christ’s at his coming—people who received the gospel in the spirit world and are judged fairly. This is the terrestrial resurrection.

f.w: that prison which is prepared for them

chapters.n: A third trumpet: the spirits of those found under condemnation.
These are “the rest of the dead,” who aren’t resurrected until the thousand years end.
A fourth trumpet: some will remain filthy even to the final day—those who refuse redemption.
A fifth trumpet: the angel carrying the everlasting gospel to every nation, people, and language.
Everyone in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will hear; every knee will bow and every tongue confess. The message: fear God and glorify him, for judgment has come.
A sixth trumpet: Babylon, who corrupted all nations, has fallen.
A seventh: “It is finished!” The Lamb has overcome, treading the winepress of God’s wrath alone.
Angels will be crowned with glory, and the Saints filled with it, receiving their inheritance and being made equal with Christ.
Then the first angel will sound again and reveal the secret deeds of people and God’s mighty works in the first thousand years of earth’s history.
The second angel will do the same for the second thousand years, revealing even hidden thoughts and intentions.

f.w: the thoughts and intents of their hearts

chapters.n: And so through the seventh, who will swear there shall be time no longer. Satan will be bound for a thousand years.

f.w: there shall be time no longer

chapters.n: Afterward he will be released for a short time to gather his armies.
Michael, the archangel—whom Latter-day Saints identify as Adam—will gather heaven’s armies.
The devil will gather the armies of hell to fight Michael.
In the battle of the great God, the devil and his armies will be cast out forever, never again to have power over the Saints.

f.w: the battle of the great God

chapters.n: Michael will fight for the Saints and defeat Satan, who seeks to take the throne of the Lamb.
This is God’s glory and that of the sanctified: they will never again see death.

f.w: shall not any more see death

chapters.n: Returning to practical matters: the Lord again commands them to call their solemn assembly.
Since not all have faith, they should teach each other wisdom from the best books and seek learning by both study and faith. This famous verse unites spiritual and intellectual learning.

f.w: seek learning, even by study and also by faith

chapters.n: Organize, prepare, and build a house—of prayer, fasting, faith, learning, glory, order, and God. This was the command to build the Kirtland Temple.

f.g: Fulfilled in the Kirtland Temple, dedicated in March 1836.

chapters.n: So that all their comings, goings, and greetings may be in the Lord’s name, with hands raised to God.
Stop shallow talk, frivolous laughter, lust, pride, light-mindedness, and all wickedness.

f.g: Treating sacred things casually or frivolously.

chapters.n: Appoint a teacher; speak one at a time and listen, so everyone is built up and has an equal chance to speak.

f.w: let one speak at a time

chapters.n: Love one another, stop being greedy, and learn to share as the gospel requires.

f.g: Greedy for what belongs to others.

chapters.n: Practical counsel: don’t be lazy, impure, or fault-finding; don’t oversleep; go to bed early and rise early so body and mind are refreshed.

f.g: Refreshed, given energy.

chapters.n: Above all, wrap yourselves in charity like a cloak; it binds everything together in perfection and peace.

f.g: Cloak or outer robe.

chapters.n: Pray always so you won’t give up, until Christ comes to receive you.

f.w: Pray always, that ye may not faint

chapters.n: Given a few days later (January 3, 1833): the order for the School of the Prophets, a school to instruct Church officers from high priests to deacons.

f.g: Began in January 1833 in an upstairs room of Newel K. Whitney’s store in Kirtland.

chapters.n: The president or teacher should be in his place in the room prepared for him.
He should be first to arrive, positioned so everyone can hear him clearly without shouting.
Arriving first is a beautiful example to the others.
He should kneel in prayer as a remembrance of the everlasting covenant.
When others come in, the teacher should rise, raise his hands to heaven, and greet them with the following words.

f.g: Greet formally.

chapters.n: The greeting is a covenant of fellowship in Christ’s name: a fixed resolve to be a friend and brother, to keep God’s commandments blamelessly, with thanksgiving forever.
Anyone unworthy of this greeting is not to be admitted, so the Lord’s house is not defiled.

f.g: Allow.

chapters.n: Faithful members entering are to return the greeting with raised hands, the same prayer and covenant, or simply by saying “Amen.”
This is a pattern for greeting one another in the house of God.

f.g: Example, model.

chapters.n: All they do there should be with prayer and thanksgiving as the Spirit directs, so the school becomes a sanctuary of the Holy Ghost.

f.g: A dwelling place; a sacred tent.

chapters.n: No one may join the school unless clean from the sins of this generation.
Members are to be received through the ordinance of washing of feet, which was established for this purpose.
The president or presiding elder performs this ordinance.
It begins with prayer and the sacrament, after which he girds himself with a towel, following Jesus’s example in John 13.

f.g: Tie a towel around his waist, as Jesus did.

f.w: the thirteenth chapter of John's testimony

chapters.n: This revelation, known as the Word of Wisdom, came after Emma Smith and others were troubled by the tobacco use in the School of the Prophets. It was addressed to the high priests in Kirtland and the Saints in Missouri.

f.g: The School of the Prophets met in the Newel K. Whitney store in Kirtland.

chapters.n: At first it was given as wise counsel, not as a strict commandment, to show God’s will for his people’s physical well-being. Later Church leaders made it a firm commandment for members.

f.g: Over time, prophets taught it as binding; today living it is required for baptism and temple worship.
Physical, earthly well-being.

chapters.n: It is a principle with a promise, simple enough for even the weakest Saint to live.

f.w: adapted to the capacity of the weak

chapters.n: God gives this warning because of the evil intentions of “conspiring men” in the last days—people who would profit from harmful substances.

f.g: Many see a fulfillment in industries that market addictive products.

chapters.n: Drinking wine or strong drink is not good or fitting before God, except for the sacrament.

f.g: Alcoholic beverages, especially distilled liquor.
Fitting, appropriate.

chapters.n: Even sacramental wine should be pure, homemade grape wine. The Lord later allowed other liquids for the sacrament; the Church today uses water.
Alcohol is not for drinking but for washing the body—as in cleaning wounds.

f.g: Stomach; i.e., for eating or drinking.

chapters.n: Tobacco is not good for the body; it has limited uses, like treating bruises or sick livestock, used with care and skill.

f.g: Smoked, chewed, or snuffed tobacco was common in 1833 America.

chapters.n: “Hot drinks” are not for the body. Early Church leaders explained this means tea and coffee, which remains the Church’s teaching.

f.g: Understood by Church leaders, beginning in the 1830s, to mean tea and coffee.

chapters.n: On the positive side, God created wholesome plants for our bodies.

f.g: Physical makeup.

chapters.n: Plants and fruits should be enjoyed in their season, with good judgment and gratitude.

f.g: Wisdom and good judgment.

chapters.n: Meat is also given by God for us to use with thanks—but sparingly.
The Lord is pleased when meat is used mainly in winter, cold, or famine.

f.g: A severe shortage of food.

chapters.n: Grain is the “staff of life”—basic food for people and animals alike.

f.g: A staple food, the support of life (like a walking staff).

chapters.n: Wild animals are made for human use only in times of famine and extreme hunger.
All grain is good food, as are fruits of the vine and whatever grows in or above the ground.
Different grains suit different uses: wheat for people, corn for oxen, oats for horses, rye for birds and pigs, and barley for animals and “mild drinks.”

f.g: In older English, often grain generally; in 1830s America, usually maize.
Probably non-intoxicating beverages made from barley.

chapters.n: Those who live this law while keeping all the commandments are promised health and strength, down to the core of their bodies.

f.w: health in their navel and marrow to their bones
walking in obedience to the commandments
f.g: The promises depend on overall faithfulness, not diet alone.

chapters.n: They will also gain wisdom and great, hidden treasures of knowledge—spiritual blessings, not only physical ones.
They will run without growing weary and walk without fainting—words from Isaiah.
The destroying angel will pass over them as it passed over Israel at the first Passover in Egypt.

f.w: the destroying angel shall pass by them

chapters.n: The Lord speaks tenderly to Joseph Smith, calling him “my son” and forgiving his sins in answer to his own prayers and his brethren’s.
Joseph is blessed as the one who holds the keys of the kingdom, which is coming forth for the last time—this is the final dispensation.
These keys will never be taken from Joseph, in this life or the next.

f.w: shall never be taken from you

chapters.n: But through Joseph the “oracles”—God’s revelations—will be given to the Church and, in time, to a successor.

f.g: Divine revelations, or the messages of God.

chapters.n: Those who receive God’s revelations must treasure them; treating them lightly brings condemnation, and they will fall when life’s storms beat on their house.
Sidney Rigdon and Frederick G. Williams are also forgiven and are counted equal with Joseph in holding the keys—the beginning of the First Presidency.
Through them also come the keys over the School of the Prophets.
The school was meant to perfect them in their ministry to bless Zion, Israel, and believing Gentiles.
Through the Presidency others receive the word and carry it to the earth’s ends—first to the Gentiles, and then to the Jews.
Then God’s power will be shown openly, convincing nations—including the house of Joseph—of the gospel.

f.w: the arm of the Lord shall be revealed

chapters.n: In that day everyone will hear the fulness of the gospel in his own language, taught by those ordained and empowered by the Holy Ghost.
The Presidency is commanded to keep serving in the ministry and in their leadership.
Once they finish revising the prophets in the Bible translation, they are to focus on presiding over the Church and the school.

f.g: Joseph’s inspired revision of the Bible (the Joseph Smith Translation), then working through the Old Testament prophets.

chapters.n: They will receive revelation, as the Spirit gives it, to unfold the mysteries of the kingdom.
They must organize the branches and learn broadly—good books, languages, and peoples. Spiritual leadership includes serious study.
Their life’s mission is to preside in council and put all Church affairs in order.
Don’t be ashamed or confused, but take warning against pride, which traps the soul.

f.g: Confused or put to shame.
Arrogance.
A trap.

chapters.n: Put your homes in order and keep laziness and impurity far away. Leadership starts at home.

f.g: Laziness.

chapters.n: A home should be found as soon as possible for Frederick G. Williams’s family.

f.g: Frederick G. Williams served as one of Joseph’s scribes.

chapters.n: Joseph Smith Sr., the Prophet’s aging father, should stay on his current farm, which was not to be sold until the Lord directed.

f.g: The Prophet’s father; later the first Presiding Patriarch.

chapters.n: Sidney Rigdon should also remain where he lives until the Lord says otherwise.
The bishop should look for an agent—a faithful man of means—to help the Church’s finances.

f.g: Savings, wealth on hand.

chapters.n: That way debts can be paid and the Lord’s storehouse won’t be disgraced in public eyes.

f.g: A bad reputation.

chapters.n: Search, pray always, and believe; all things will work together for good if they live uprightly and keep their covenants with one another.

f.w: all things shall work together for your good

chapters.n: They should keep their households small, especially Joseph Sr.’s, by not taking in too many people outside the family.
Otherwise the resources meant for the Lord’s work could be drained by those not worthy of them.
That would hinder them from doing what God commanded.
Vienna Jaques, a faithful convert who had consecrated her savings, should receive money for her travel to Zion.

f.g: A convert from Boston who donated much of her savings to the Church; she later traveled to Utah.
Female servant—a respectful scriptural term for a faithful woman.

chapters.n: The rest of her money is consecrated to the Lord, and he promises to reward her.

f.g: The remainder.

chapters.n: It is right that she go to Zion and receive an inheritance from the bishop.
There she may settle in peace if faithful, and keep busy all her days.
Joseph should write to the Saints in Zion that the Presidency is called to preside over Zion too, in the Lord’s timing.
Those in Zion should stop pestering the Lord about this question.
The Saints in Zion are beginning to repent, and angels rejoice.
Still, the Lord is displeased with much, including William E. McLellin, Sidney Gilbert, the bishop, and others who need to repent.
The Lord will contend with Zion and correct her leaders until she overcomes and is clean.

f.g: Correct through discipline.

chapters.n: Zion will not be moved from its appointed place. The Lord has spoken it.

f.w: she shall not be removed out of her place

chapters.n: Joseph Smith’s Bible contained the Apocrypha, books found in some Bibles but not in the Hebrew scriptures. He asked whether to revise them. The Lord answers that they contain much truth and are mostly translated correctly.

f.g: From Greek “hidden”; Jewish writings such as 1–2 Maccabees, Tobit, and Judith, included in Catholic and some Protestant Bibles.

chapters.n: They also contain things that aren’t true—additions inserted by people over time.

f.g: Words or passages inserted into a text by later hands.

chapters.n: It isn’t necessary for Joseph to make an inspired revision of the Apocrypha.
Whoever reads it should read with understanding, because the Spirit reveals what is true.
A person guided by the Spirit will benefit from reading it.
Someone without the Spirit won’t benefit. This principle applies to all reading—the Spirit helps us sort truth from error.
The Lord instructs the united order (the United Firm) to receive Frederick G. Williams, newly called to the First Presidency, as a member. What he says to one applies to all.

f.g: The United Firm, a group of leaders managing Church business enterprises.

chapters.n: Frederick is to be a “lively”—active, energetic—member. If he keeps the commandments, he will be blessed forever.

f.g: Active, energetic, engaged.

chapters.n: A wonderful promise: everyone who forsakes sin, comes to Christ, prays, obeys, and keeps his commandments will see his face and know that he lives.
They will know he is the true light given to every person born into the world.

f.w: the true light that lighteth every man

chapters.n: And that he is in the Father and the Father in him—they are one in purpose and glory.

f.w: the Father and I are one

chapters.n: Christ explains why he is called both Father and Son: the Father gave him of his fulness, and he became the Son by taking a mortal body and living among people.

f.g: Took a physical body as his dwelling.

chapters.n: While on earth he received from the Father, and the Father’s works were clearly shown through him.
John saw and testified of Christ’s full glory. A fuller version of John’s record will be revealed later.

f.g: Many believe this refers to John the Baptist, whose record seems to underlie the opening of John’s Gospel; others think John the Apostle. The text does not say.

chapters.n: John testifies that he saw Christ’s glory, and that Christ existed before the world was made.

f.w: in the beginning, before the world was

chapters.n: Christ was “the Word”—the messenger who brings salvation.

f.g: Greek Logos: the one who reveals and expresses God.

chapters.n: He is the light and Redeemer of the world and the Spirit of truth. He came into the world he created, and in him is the life and light of humanity.

f.w: the world was made by him

chapters.n: He created worlds, people, and all things.

f.w: The worlds were made by him

chapters.n: John bears witness that he saw Christ’s glory as the Only Begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth, living in mortal flesh among them.
A profound teaching: Jesus did not receive God’s fulness all at once but grew “grace for grace.”

f.g: Receiving grace step by step, perhaps by giving grace to others in turn.

chapters.n: He kept growing from grace to grace until he received a fulness. Even the Savior progressed line upon line.
That is why he was called the Son of God—because he grew into the fulness rather than starting with it.
At his baptism the heavens opened, the Holy Ghost descended like a dove, and the Father declared, “This is my beloved Son.”

f.w: in the form of a dove

chapters.n: He then received a fulness of the Father’s glory.
He received all power in heaven and on earth, and the Father’s glory dwelt in him.

f.w: all power, both in heaven and on earth

chapters.n: If faithful, the Saints will receive John’s full record. It has not yet been revealed.
These teachings explain how and whom we worship, so we can come to the Father through Christ and eventually receive his fulness.

f.w: know how to worship, and know what you worship

chapters.n: Keeping the commandments leads us along the same path Jesus walked—grace for grace—until we too receive the Father’s fulness.

f.w: be glorified in me as I am in the Father

chapters.n: Christ was with the Father from the beginning and is the Firstborn of God’s spirit children.
Those spiritually born through him share his glory and form the Church of the Firstborn.
We too were with the Father in the beginning, as spirits.

f.w: Ye were also in the beginning with the Father

chapters.n: A famous definition: truth is knowledge of things as they are, were, and will be.

f.w: truth is knowledge of things as they are

chapters.n: Anything that adds to or takes away from truth comes from Satan, who has been a liar from the beginning.
The Spirit of truth comes from God; Christ is that Spirit, and John testified he received all truth.

f.w: I am the Spirit of truth

chapters.n: No one receives a fulness without keeping God’s commandments.
Obedience brings truth and light, more and more, until one is glorified and knows all things.
People also existed with God in the beginning. Intelligence—the light of truth—was never created and cannot be. Our core self is eternal.

f.g: The eternal essence or core of a person’s spirit.

chapters.n: Truth and intelligence are free to act within the sphere God has given them; without that agency nothing would truly exist.
This is human agency—and also the basis of accountability: truth is plainly shown, yet people reject the light.
Anyone whose spirit refuses the light is under condemnation.
People are spirit; the elements are eternal. When spirit and body are permanently united in resurrection, they receive a fulness of joy.

f.g: Matter is eternal; God organized creation rather than making it from nothing.

chapters.n: Separated—as in death—a person cannot have a fulness of joy. This is why the body matters so much.
The body is a temple of God; whoever defiles that temple will face destruction.

f.w: man is the tabernacle of God

chapters.n: A defining verse, later adopted as Brigham Young University’s motto: God’s glory is intelligence—light and truth.

f.w: The glory of God is intelligence

chapters.n: Light and truth always abandon Satan.
Every spirit began innocent. Through Christ’s redemption from the Fall, children are born innocent before God.
Satan takes away light and truth through disobedience and through false traditions handed down by parents.
So God commands parents to raise children in light and truth.

f.w: bring up your children in light and truth

chapters.n: The Lord now corrects specific leaders. Frederick G. Williams has been under condemnation.
He has not taught his children as commanded, and Satan has power over him—the cause of his troubles.
To be freed he must set his own house in order.

f.w: set in order your own house

chapters.n: Sidney Rigdon too has neglected some commandments about his children and must first set his house in order.
Even before correcting Joseph, Christ calls the leaders friends who will inherit with him.
He called them servants for the world’s sake, and they serve the world for his sake.
Even Joseph Smith is rebuked for not keeping the commandments. Prophets are not exempt from correction.
Joseph’s family must repent, give more heed to his words, or lose their place.
This applies to all: pray always, so Satan doesn’t gain power and remove you from your place.
Bishop Newel K. Whitney must also be corrected; his family must be more diligent at home and pray always.

f.g: Corrected, disciplined.

chapters.n: Sidney Rigdon should go on his mission quickly to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord. The others’ united prayers of faith will uphold him.

f.g: The time of the Lord’s favor and deliverance.

chapters.n: Joseph and Frederick should also hurry; their prayers of faith will be answered, and those who keep God’s words will not be put to shame in this world or the next.

f.g: Put to shame.

chapters.n: They should hurry to finish the Bible translation and also learn history, geography, nations, and law—all for Zion’s salvation.

f.g: The Joseph Smith Translation of the Bible, largely completed in July 1833.

chapters.n: The Lord commands the Saints to begin laying out Kirtland as a city—a stake of Zion—starting from the site of his house, the temple.

f.w: the city of the stake of Zion

f.g: The Kirtland Temple, then in early planning.

chapters.n: It must follow the pattern God gave, as Moses built the tabernacle by divine pattern.
The first lot south of the temple is to hold a building for the First Presidency’s work, including receiving revelation and ministering to the Church.

f.g: This building was never constructed, largely due to persecution and lack of funds.

chapters.n: It is to measure 55 by 65 feet inside—the same dimensions as the temple.

f.g: The interior space.

chapters.n: It will have a lower and an upper room, with details to come later.
It must be dedicated to the Lord from its foundation, according to the priesthood order.
The building is wholly devoted to the work of the Presidency.
Nothing unclean may enter, so the Lord’s glory and presence can dwell there.
If anything unclean enters, his glory and presence will not come. Holiness invites God’s presence.
The second lot south is for a printing house to publish the Bible translation and other things the Lord commands.

f.w: the printing of the translation of my scriptures
f.g: The Joseph Smith Translation was not published in full during Joseph’s lifetime.

chapters.n: It too will be 55 by 65 feet with lower and upper rooms.
Even a print shop is to be wholly dedicated, holy, and undefiled—sacred work can happen in practical places.

f.g: Pure, not made unclean.

chapters.n: Hyrum Smith, the Prophet’s older brother, is to receive his inheritance on the third lot.
Reynolds Cahoon and Jared Carter receive the first two lots on the north side.

f.g: With Hyrum Smith, they formed the committee to build the Kirtland Temple.

chapters.n: These three men serve as the building committee for the Lord’s houses.

f.w: a committee to build mine houses

chapters.n: The two buildings are not to be started until the Lord commands it.
Nothing more is given at this time.

Five months after commanding a temple, construction hadn’t begun. The Lord corrects the Saints—but first says he loves them. He chastens those he loves, to forgive them and help them escape temptation.

f.w: whom I love I also chasten

chapters.n: So they must be corrected and rebuked before him.
Their serious sin was neglecting the great commandment to build his house.

f.g: Very serious, causing grief.

chapters.n: The temple would prepare the apostles to prune his vineyard a final time, so he can do his “strange act” and pour his Spirit on all people.

f.w: prune my vineyard for the last time

f.g: God’s unusual work—here the restoration and the gathering.

f.w: pour out my Spirit upon all flesh

chapters.n: Many have been ordained, but few are chosen.

f.w: called but few of them are chosen

chapters.n: Those not chosen are “walking in darkness at noon-day”—missing light that is all around them.
That is why he commanded a solemn assembly, so their fasting and mourning could reach the Lord of Sabaoth—which the revelation interprets as “the creator of the first day.”

f.g: Hebrew for Lord of Hosts; this verse gives an additional interpretation linking it to God as Creator.

chapters.n: The house was to be where God would endow his chosen servants “with power from on high.”

f.g: Give a gift; here a spiritual empowerment.

chapters.n: This is the Father’s promise, so they must wait for it, as the apostles waited in Jerusalem before Pentecost.
Some servants sinned seriously, and arguments arose in the School of the Prophets, which grieved the Lord, so he sent them out to be chastened.

f.g: Quarrels, disputes.

chapters.n: God wants them to build the house. If they keep his commandments, they will have power to build it.

f.w: you shall have power to build it

chapters.n: If not, they will lose the Father’s love and walk in darkness.
The house must not be built the world’s way, because they are not to live like the world.

f.w: not after the manner of the world

chapters.n: It will be built after a pattern shown to three men they appoint. Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams later reported seeing the building in vision.

f.g: The First Presidency: Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams.

chapters.n: Its interior is to be 55 feet wide and 65 feet long.
The lower room is for the sacrament, preaching, fasting, prayer, and offering the Saints’ most holy desires.
The upper room is for the school of the apostles. The Lord names himself Son Ahman, Alphus, and Omegus—Jesus Christ.

f.g: Early Church leaders taught that “Ahman” is a name of God the Father, so Son Ahman means the Son of God.
A form of Alpha—the first.

chapters.n: Leaders were unsure how to handle the Peter French farm, purchased for the temple site. The Lord says this stake of Zion must be made strong.

f.g: Kirtland, Ohio, a support to Zion in Missouri.

chapters.n: Bishop Newel K. Whitney is to take charge of the property where the temple will be built.

f.w: the place which is named among you
f.g: The French farm, bought by the Church in Kirtland in 1833.

chapters.n: The land should be divided into lots wisely for those needing inheritances, as decided in council.
They should set apart a portion for the “order” (the United Firm) to help publish God’s word.
Spreading God’s word is most important to the Lord, because it softens hearts—which also helps the Saints.

f.g: Softening or winning over people’s hearts.

chapters.n: John Johnson of Hiram, Ohio—who had hosted Joseph Smith—has had his offering accepted. He is promised eternal life if he keeps the commandments.

f.g: A farmer in Hiram, Ohio, whose home Joseph used while revising the Bible and receiving many revelations.

chapters.n: He is a descendant of Joseph of Egypt and an heir to the blessings promised to his ancestors.
He is to join the order to help bring forth God’s word.
He should be set apart for this and work to clear the debts on the property so he can live there.

f.g: Debts or legal claims against a property.

chapters.n: Speaking by his Spirit, the Lord reveals his will for the Saints in Missouri. Many there are humble and earnestly seeking wisdom. News of the July 1833 mob attacks in Independence had not yet reached Kirtland.

f.g: Jackson County, Missouri.

chapters.n: Such humble seekers are blessed. The Lord shows mercy to the meek and to whom he chooses, and his judgment will be fair.
He is pleased with the “school in Zion” and with its leader, Parley P. Pratt, who stays close to the Lord.

f.g: A Missouri counterpart to Kirtland’s School of the Prophets, held in the open air.

chapters.n: Parley will keep leading the school as long as he remains faithful.

f.g: Parley P. Pratt, an early missionary and later apostle, taught about sixty elders in this school.

chapters.n: He will be greatly blessed in explaining the scriptures and deep truths to build up the school and Church.

f.g: A great number.
Explaining in detail.

chapters.n: The Lord will be merciful to the rest, though some must be corrected and their deeds exposed.

f.w: their works shall be made known

chapters.n: Quoting John the Baptist: the ax is ready at the tree’s root; any tree without good fruit will be cut down and burned.

f.w: The ax is laid at the root of the trees

chapters.n: Those whose hearts are honest, broken, and contrite, and who are willing to keep their covenants through any sacrifice the Lord asks, are accepted by him.

f.g: Humbly sorry for sin; teachable.

chapters.n: God will make them like a fruitful tree planted by a pure stream in good soil, bearing precious fruit.
A temple is to be built in Zion according to the pattern already given.

f.w: a house should be built unto me

chapters.n: It should be built quickly, funded by the Saints’ tithing.

f.g: In 1833 this meant freewill offerings in general; the tenth-of-increase law came in 1838.

chapters.n: This is the offering and sacrifice the Lord asks, so a house can be built for Zion’s salvation.
The temple would be a place of thanksgiving for all Saints and of instruction for all called to serve.
There they would be perfected in understanding their ministries—in theory, principle, and doctrine—through the keys given to them.

f.w: in theory, in principle, and in doctrine

chapters.n: If the people build in the Lord’s name and keep it clean, his glory will rest on it.

f.w: my glory shall rest upon it

chapters.n: His presence will be there, and the pure in heart who enter will see God.
But if it is defiled, he will not come, for he does not dwell in unholy temples.
If Zion obeys, she will prosper, expand, and become glorious, great, and “terrible”—awe-inspiring.

f.g: Awe-inspiring, commanding respect.

chapters.n: Nations will honor Zion as God’s city, unshakable because God is there.
God has sworn to be her salvation and her high tower—a refuge.

f.g: A fortified lookout; a place of safety.

chapters.n: A defining statement: Zion is “the pure in heart.” Zion is first a condition of the people, then a place.
Vengeance comes suddenly on the ungodly like a whirlwind; who can escape?
The Lord’s scourge will continue night and day, and its news will trouble everyone until the Lord comes.

f.g: A source of punishment or affliction.

chapters.n: God’s anger burns against wickedness and abominations.
Yet Zion will escape if she does all the Lord commands.
If not, she will face severe affliction—disease, plague, war, and fire. Within months the Saints were driven from Jackson County.

f.w: I will visit her according to all her works

chapters.n: Still, the Lord has accepted Zion’s offering; if she sins no more, none of these things will come.
He will multiply blessings upon her and her generations forever.
Given just after news arrived of mob violence against the Saints in Missouri. The Lord comforts his friends: don’t fear, rejoice always, and give thanks in everything.
Wait patiently on the Lord. Their prayers have reached him and are recorded with a seal; he has sworn they will be granted.

f.g: Lord of Hosts.

chapters.n: He makes an unchangeable covenant: everything they suffer will work together for their good and his glory.

f.g: Unchangeable.

chapters.n: Concerning civil law: his people should do all he commands.
Constitutional law that protects freedom, rights, and privileges belongs to all humanity and is approved by God.

f.g: Consistent with the U.S. Constitution, which protects individual liberties.

chapters.n: So the Saints are justified in supporting constitutional law.

f.g: Supporting, upholding.

chapters.n: Any human law that goes beyond or falls short of this principle of freedom comes from evil.
God makes people free, and good law also protects that freedom.
But when the wicked rule, people mourn.

f.w: when the wicked rule the people mourn

chapters.n: So seek out and support honest, wise, and good leaders.
Forsake all evil, hold to all good, and live by every word of God.

f.w: every word which proceedeth forth out of the mouth of God

chapters.n: God teaches the faithful step by step—line upon line—and will test them with this knowledge.

f.w: line upon line, precept upon precept

f.g: Test.

chapters.n: Whoever gives his life for Christ’s cause will find eternal life.
Don’t fear enemies. God will test them in all things to see whether they will keep his covenant even to death.
Those who won’t keep his covenant are not worthy of him.
A key command: renounce war and proclaim peace. Work to turn the hearts of children and parents toward each other.

f.w: turn the hearts of the children to their fathers

chapters.n: And turn the hearts of the Jews to the prophets and the prophets to the Jews, lest the earth be cursed and consumed.

f.w: smite the whole earth with a curse

chapters.n: Echoing Jesus’s Last Supper words: don’t be troubled—there are many mansions in the Father’s house, and a place prepared for you.

f.w: in my Father's house are many mansions

chapters.n: The Lord is displeased with many Saints in Kirtland.
They haven’t forsaken their sins, pride, greed, and wicked ways, nor followed his words of wisdom and life.

f.g: Greed; desire for what others have.

chapters.n: He will discipline them as he sees fit if they don’t repent.

f.g: Whatever I choose.

chapters.n: If they obey, he will turn away all wrath, and the gates of hell will not prevail against them.

f.w: the gates of hell shall not prevail

chapters.n: Now the law of retaliation and forgiveness. If someone strikes them or their families once and they bear it patiently without insulting back or seeking revenge, they will be rewarded.

f.g: Don’t respond with abusive words.

chapters.n: If they don’t bear it patiently, their suffering will be counted as a fair consequence rather than rewarded.

f.w: meted out as a just measure
f.g: Given as a deserved portion.

chapters.n: If struck a second time and they bear it patiently, their reward will be a hundredfold.
A third time, borne patiently, doubles their reward fourfold.
These three instances stand as witnesses against the enemy if he doesn’t repent.
If the enemy escapes judgment, they should warn him in the Lord’s name to leave them and their descendants alone.
If he attacks again after the warning, God has delivered him into their hands.
If they choose to spare him, they and their descendants will be rewarded for their righteousness.
Still, they would be justified in responding to him as his deeds deserve, especially if their lives are in danger. Self-defense is permitted.
This is the same law God gave Nephi, Joseph, Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, and the ancient prophets and apostles.
God’s ancient people were not to go to war against anyone unless he commanded it.

f.w: save I, the Lord, commanded them

chapters.n: If anyone declared war on them, they were first to raise a banner of peace.

f.g: A flag or banner offering peace.

chapters.n: If the peace offer was refused three times, they were to bring those witnesses before the Lord.
Then God would command them and justify going to battle.
And he would fight their battles and their descendants’ battles.

f.w: I, the Lord, would fight their battles

chapters.n: This is an example for all people of what God considers justified.

f.g: Example.

chapters.n: If an enemy who struck them once repents and asks forgiveness, they must forgive and no longer hold it against him.
And so on as often as he repents—up to seventy times seven, as Jesus taught.
Even if he wrongs them once and does not repent, they must still forgive.
Likewise the second time, though unrepentant.
And the third time.
But on the fourth unrepented offense they should bring it before the Lord, where it remains until the offender repents and makes fourfold restitution.

f.g: Restitution of four times the loss, as in the law of Moses for some thefts.

chapters.n: If he does, they must forgive him wholeheartedly. If not, the Lord will avenge them.

f.w: forgive him with all thine heart

chapters.n: That vengeance can extend to his descendants who also hate God.

f.w: of all them that hate me

chapters.n: But if those descendants repent with all their heart, might, mind, and strength and make restitution, the anger is turned away.

f.w: with all their hearts and with all their might, mind, and strength

chapters.n: Vengeance will end, and their wrongs will never again be held against them. God’s mercy reaches every generation that repents.

Given in August 1832 (placed here out of date order). John Murdock, a widower whose wife died after giving birth to twins, is called to preach in the eastern states from house to house despite persecution.

f.g: His infant twins were adopted by Joseph and Emma Smith after their own twins died in 1831.
Eastern regions of the United States.

chapters.n: Whoever receives him receives the Lord, and he will preach with the Spirit’s convincing power.
Those who receive him with childlike humility receive the kingdom and will find mercy.
Those who reject him will be rejected by the Father. He should privately cleanse his feet as a witness against them.
Christ is coming quickly to judgment to convict people of their ungodly deeds, as written of him in scripture.

f.w: to convince all of their ungodly deeds

chapters.n: He should not leave until his children are cared for and lovingly sent to the bishop in Zion.
After a few years, if he wishes, he may go to Zion to receive his inheritance.
Otherwise he will keep preaching until he dies.

f.g: Until death.

chapters.n: Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon were on a mission to Upper Canada and stopped in Perrysburg, New York, worried about their families. The Lord reassures them: their families are well and in his hands.

f.w: in me there is all power

chapters.n: So they should follow him and listen to his counsel.
He has many people in this region, and an effective door for the gospel will open in the East.

f.w: I have much people in this place

f.g: An opening that leads to real results.

chapters.n: He allowed them to come here because it served the salvation of souls.

f.g: Allowed.

chapters.n: They should speak boldly, saying the thoughts he puts in their hearts, and they won’t be put to shame.

f.w: speak the thoughts that I shall put into your hearts

chapters.n: They will be given what to say at the very moment it’s needed.
But they must teach in his name with seriousness of heart and gentle meekness.
If they do, the Holy Ghost will bear witness to everything they say.

f.w: the Holy Ghost shall be shed forth

chapters.n: Sidney is called to be a spokesman for Joseph, much as Aaron spoke for Moses.
Joseph will be given power to bear mighty testimony.
Sidney will be powerful in explaining scripture; Joseph will be a revelator to him, so Sidney can know with certainty the truths of the kingdom.

f.g: Explaining in detail.
One who receives and makes known revelation from God.

chapters.n: They should continue their journey joyfully, for the Lord is with them to the end.

f.w: I am with you even unto the end

chapters.n: About Zion: it will be redeemed, even though it is being chastened for a while. The Saints were being driven out of Jackson County at this very time.

f.g: A short period.

chapters.n: Orson Hyde and John Gould, sent to Missouri with messages, are in the Lord’s hands and will be saved if faithful.

f.g: Messengers sent from Kirtland to counsel the Missouri Saints in 1833.

chapters.n: Take comfort: all things work together for good for those who live uprightly and to make the Church holy.

f.w: all things shall work together for good

chapters.n: The Lord will raise up a pure people who serve him in righteousness.
All who call on the Lord’s name and keep his commandments will be saved.

f.w: call upon the name of the Lord

chapters.n: In late 1833 mobs drove over a thousand Saints from Jackson County, Missouri. The Lord now speaks about those who were persecuted and expelled from their promised land.

f.w: cast out from the land of their inheritance
f.g: In November 1833 the Saints fled across the Missouri River into Clay County.

chapters.n: He allowed this suffering because of their sins.
Yet he will claim them as his own, his treasured “jewels,” when he comes.

f.g: Gather his treasured possessions.

chapters.n: They must be tried, as Abraham was tested when asked to offer Isaac.
Those who will not endure correction but deny God cannot be made holy.

f.g: Correction, discipline.

chapters.n: There had been quarreling, envy, strife, lust, and greed among them, which polluted their inheritances.

f.g: Clashes, disagreements.
Greedy.

chapters.n: They were slow to listen to God, so he is slow to answer their prayers in trouble.
In peaceful times they took his counsel lightly; in trouble, they reached for him because they had to.
Despite their sins, God’s heart is full of compassion. He won’t cast them off, and in wrath he will remember mercy.

f.w: my bowels are filled with compassion
f.g: “Bowels” meant the inner seat of feelings.

f.w: in the day of wrath I will remember mercy

chapters.n: As promised before, he will let his sword of judgment fall on behalf of his people.
His anger will be poured out on all nations when their wickedness is complete.

f.w: the cup of their iniquity is full

chapters.n: In that day all who are found watching—all of covenant Israel—will be saved.

f.g: A tall lookout post; here a symbol of spiritual vigilance.

chapters.n: The scattered will be gathered.

f.w: they that have been scattered shall be gathered

chapters.n: Those who mourn will be comforted.

f.w: they who have mourned shall be comforted

chapters.n: Those who gave their lives for him will be crowned.
So take comfort about Zion; everyone is in God’s hands. “Be still and know that I am God.”

f.w: be still and know that I am God

chapters.n: Zion will not be moved from its place, though its people are scattered.

f.w: Zion shall not be moved out of her place

chapters.n: The pure in heart who remain will return with their children, singing everlasting joy, to rebuild Zion’s ruins.
All this will happen to fulfill the prophets.
No other place is appointed as Zion’s center for gathering.
Until there is no more room; then other places, called stakes, will be appointed as the “curtains” or strength of Zion.

f.g: Like stakes holding up a tent, these strengthen Zion.
The fabric of a tent—Zion pictured as an expanding tent.

chapters.n: All who worship God according to his gospel should gather and stand in holy places.
They should prepare for the day when the veil covering the earth is removed and everyone sees the Lord together.

f.w: all flesh shall see me together

chapters.n: Every corruptible thing—people, animals, birds, fish—will be consumed.

f.g: Subject to decay; also, morally corrupt.

chapters.n: The elements will melt with intense heat, and all things will be made new so God’s knowledge and glory fill the earth.
Hostility between people and between animals will end. This is the Millennium.

f.g: Hostility, hatred.

chapters.n: Whatever anyone asks will be given.
Satan will have no power to tempt.
There will be no sorrow, because there is no death as we know it.
Infants will not die young; lifespans will be like a tree’s.

f.w: as the age of a tree

chapters.n: When people die they will not lie in the grave but be changed instantly—resurrected—and enter a glorious rest.

f.w: changed in the twinkling of an eye

chapters.n: When the Lord comes, he will reveal all things.
Past events, hidden things, how the earth was made, and its purpose and end.
Most precious truths about heaven, earth, and everything in them.
Those persecuted for his name who endure in faith—even unto death—will share all this glory.
So don’t fear even death. In this world joy is incomplete, but in Christ it is full.

f.w: in me your joy is full

chapters.n: Care more for the soul than for the body and its life.
Seek the Lord’s face always; through patience they will keep their souls and gain eternal life.

f.w: in patience ye may possess your souls
seek the face of the Lord

chapters.n: Those who make covenants with God become the “salt of the earth.”

f.g: Flavor, taste—salt that preserves and seasons.

chapters.n: If salt loses its flavor, it is useless and thrown out. Covenant people must stay true to bless others.

f.w: trodden under the feet of men

chapters.n: Many (not all) of Zion’s people had transgressed and needed correction.
Those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and the humble will be lifted up.

f.w: He that exalteth himself shall be abased

f.g: Humbled, brought low.

chapters.n: Now a parable about Zion’s redemption.
A nobleman had a choice piece of land and told servants to plant twelve olive trees on it.

f.g: Olive trees often symbolize the house of Israel; twelve may suggest Israel’s tribes.

chapters.n: They were to set watchmen and build a tower to see enemies coming and protect the vineyard.
The servants planted the trees, built a hedge, set watchmen, and began the tower.

f.g: A protective fence of shrubs or a wall.

chapters.n: But while laying the foundation, they began to question: why does our lord need a tower?
They debated at length: it’s a time of peace—why build it?
Couldn’t the money go to the moneychangers (to earn interest)? It seemed unnecessary.

f.g: Bankers or moneylenders who would pay interest.

chapters.n: Arguing among themselves, they became lazy and stopped obeying.

f.g: In disagreement.
Lazy.

chapters.n: The enemy came at night, broke down the hedge, and the frightened servants fled while the olive trees were destroyed.

f.g: Frightened.

chapters.n: The nobleman demanded: what caused this disaster?
Shouldn’t they have obeyed, built the tower, set a watchman, and stayed awake?
A watchman on the tower would have seen the enemy far off, giving time to prepare and save the vineyard. Obedience to seemingly unnecessary commands can be protective.
The lord tells one servant to gather the strength of his house—young and middle-aged men—except those told to stay.

f.g: The Lord later identified Joseph Smith as this servant.

chapters.n: They are to go quickly and redeem the vineyard, for he bought it with money.

f.w: I have bought it with money

chapters.n: Break down the enemies’ walls, throw down their tower, and scatter their watchmen.
If enemies gather against them, avenge the lord, so he can later come with the rest of his household and possess the land.
The servant asks when this will happen.
“When I will.” Go now and do all I command.
This is his seal and blessing: to be a faithful and wise steward and a ruler in the kingdom.
The servant obeyed, and after many days all was fulfilled. This parable set the stage for Zion’s Camp in 1834.
The Lord now gives wisdom for all the branches willing to be guided rightly.
The gathering must continue so the Saints can be built up in holy places; harvest time has come.

f.w: the time of harvest is come

chapters.n: As in the parable of the wheat and tares, the wheat will be gathered into barns for eternal life and celestial glory.

f.w: the parable of the wheat and the tares

f.g: Granaries, storehouses for grain.

chapters.n: The tares will be bound tightly in bundles to be burned.
All branches should keep gathering to the appointed places.
But not in haste or by fleeing—prepare everything first.

f.w: let not your gathering be in haste

chapters.n: To be prepared, follow the earlier commandment about land.
Buy with money all available land around the area appointed as Zion.

f.w: purchase all the lands with money

chapters.n: All land that can be bought in Jackson County and nearby counties; leave the rest to God.
Branches should pool their money and act in due time, not hastily, with everything prepared.
Honorable, wise men should be appointed to purchase lands.
Eastern branches, once strong, could also buy land and gather there, building Zion.
There are already enough resources to redeem Zion—if the churches bearing Christ’s name would listen.
The scattered Saints should keep appealing for justice to those in authority.

f.g: Plead persistently.
Compensation or remedy for a wrong.

chapters.n: According to the laws and Constitution, which God allowed to be established to protect the rights of all people.

f.w: for the rights and protection of all flesh

chapters.n: So everyone can act on religious belief by their God-given agency and be accountable for their own sins.
So no one should be in bondage to another.
God established the U.S. Constitution through wise men he raised up, and redeemed the land through bloodshed (the Revolution).

f.w: I established the Constitution of this land

chapters.n: The Saints are compared to Jesus’s parable of the persistent widow and the unjust judge, which teaches always to pray and not give up.

f.w: men ought always to pray and not to faint

chapters.n: A judge in a city neither feared God nor cared about people.
A widow kept asking him for justice against her adversary.

f.g: Give me justice.

chapters.n: Eventually he granted it, not from virtue, but because her persistence wore him down.
So will it be with Zion’s children.
They should plead with the judge.
If ignored, with the governor.

f.g: The Saints appealed to Missouri governor Daniel Dunklin.

chapters.n: If ignored, with the president of the United States.

f.g: Appeals were later made to Presidents Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren.

chapters.n: If the president ignores them, the Lord will arise from his hiding place and trouble the nation.
In his time he will cut off wicked, unjust stewards and assign them a place with hypocrites and unbelievers.
In outer darkness, with weeping and gnashing of teeth.
So pray that leaders will hear, so God can be merciful to them.
These things must happen so all are left without excuse.
So wise men and rulers can hear what they never considered.

f.w: that which they have never considered

chapters.n: So God can bring about his “strange act” and “strange work,” making clear the difference between righteous and wicked.

f.w: discern between the righteous and the wicked

chapters.n: Sidney Gilbert should not sell the storehouse in Independence to enemies.

f.g: A. Sidney Gilbert ran the Church store in Independence.

chapters.n: What God appointed should not be handed to enemies with members’ consent.
That would be a serious sin given what is soon to happen among the nations.
The Saints should keep their legal claim on their lands even though they can’t live there now.
Yet if they bring forth fruit worthy of the kingdom, they shall live there.

f.g: Fitting works.

chapters.n: They will build and inhabit; plant vineyards and eat the fruit—Isaiah’s promise for God’s people.

f.w: they shall plant vineyards, and they shall eat the fruit thereof

chapters.n: These are minutes, not a voice-of-the-Lord revelation. On February 17, 1834, twenty-four high priests met at Joseph Smith’s home in Kirtland and organized the Church’s first high council: twelve high priests plus a presidency.

f.w: general council of twenty-four high priests
f.g: These minutes were recorded by clerks Oliver Cowdery and Orson Hyde and later revised by Joseph Smith.
A council of twelve high priests; stakes today still have high councils.

chapters.n: The high council would settle serious problems that local members or the bishop’s council couldn’t resolve to everyone’s satisfaction.

The First Presidency—Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Frederick G. Williams—presided, and twelve high priests, including Joseph Smith Sr., Martin Harris, and Oliver Cowdery, were chosen unanimously as standing councilors.

f.g: A permanent council in one location, unlike a temporary or traveling one.

chapters.n: Each man was asked if he accepted the call and would serve according to heaven’s law. All agreed, relying on God’s grace.

f.w: according to the grace of God

chapters.n: Forty-three people voted for the Church in sustaining them: high priests, elders, priests, and members. Common consent was already central.

f.g: An early example of the principle of common consent.

chapters.n: At least seven councilors (or their replacements) must be present for the council to act—a quorum.

f.w: cannot have power to act without seven
f.g: A quorum—the minimum number needed to act officially.

chapters.n: Those seven may appoint other worthy high priests to fill in for absent members.
Permanent vacancies—from death, removal for sin, or moving away—are filled by the president’s nomination and sustained by a council of high priests.

f.g: The geographic area under this council’s authority.

chapters.n: The president of the Church also presides over this council. He is called by revelation and sustained by the Church’s vote.
It befits his office to preside, assisted by two other presidents appointed the same way.

f.g: Rank, honor of position.

chapters.n: If one or both counselors are absent, he can preside alone; if he is absent, either counselor may preside.
Councilors draw numbered lots, 1–12, to determine the order in which they speak.

f.g: Draw randomly; today councilors’ numbers are usually based on seniority or assigned seats.

chapters.n: For a simple case, only two councilors speak.
Harder cases have four speakers, and the hardest six—never more.
The accused always has half the council assigned to protect him from insult or injustice—a principle of fairness.

f.g: Here, abusive treatment or unfair attack.

chapters.n: Speakers present the case truthfully after reviewing evidence, speaking with fairness and justice.

f.g: Fairness, impartiality.

chapters.n: Even-numbered councilors stand for the accused; odd-numbered present the other side.
Both the accuser and the accused may speak for themselves after the evidence and councilors.
Then the president renders a decision and asks the councilors to sustain it by vote.

f.g: Approve, confirm.

chapters.n: If any councilor who hasn’t spoken sees an error in the decision, he can say so and the case is reheard.
If the rehearing brings new light, the decision changes accordingly.
If not, the original decision stands, with the majority confirming it.
If a doctrinal question isn’t clear from existing scripture, the president may seek the Lord’s will by revelation.

f.w: obtain the mind of the Lord by revelation

chapters.n: High priests away from Church headquarters may form a similar council to settle disputes when requested.

f.g: Away from Church headquarters; in outlying areas.

chapters.n: Such a council may choose one of its members to preside temporarily.
It must promptly send a full record of its proceedings and testimony to the high council at the First Presidency’s headquarters.

f.g: Send.

chapters.n: Dissatisfied parties may appeal to that high council, which hears the case afresh.

f.g: Request a higher body to review a decision.

chapters.n: These outlying councils are only for the most difficult cases, not ordinary matters.
Local high priests decide whether calling such a council is necessary.
There’s a difference between these local or traveling high priests’ councils and the traveling high council of the Twelve Apostles.

f.g: The Quorum of the Twelve was organized in 1835; this wording was added when the minutes were published that year.

chapters.n: Decisions of the former can be appealed; decisions of the Twelve cannot.
The Twelve can be called into question only by the general authorities, and only in case of transgression.

f.g: Leaders with Church-wide authority.

chapters.n: The First Presidency decides whether an appealed case deserves a rehearing after examining the evidence.
The twelve councilors drew lots to set their speaking order; the list records the result. The meeting closed with prayer.

f.g: Ended the meeting.

chapters.n: Parley P. Pratt and Lyman Wight had come from Missouri to ask how to help the exiled Saints. The Lord now gives instructions for redeeming his scattered people in Zion.

f.w: scattered on the land of Zion
f.g: Expelled from Jackson County in late 1833.
