chapters.n: They were driven and beaten by enemies, on whom God will pour his wrath in his own time.

f.g: Struck, beaten.

chapters.n: God allowed this so the persecutors’ wickedness would reach its full measure.

f.w: fill up the measure of their iniquities

chapters.n: It also chastened the Saints, who had not fully obeyed his commandments.
God has issued a decree that his people will see fulfilled if they obey from this hour.
They will begin to prevail over enemies starting now.
If they obey, they will keep prevailing until the world’s kingdoms are subdued and the earth is given to the Saints forever.

f.w: the earth is given unto the saints

chapters.n: If they don’t, the world’s kingdoms will prevail against them.
They were meant to be a light to the world and saviors of others.
If they don’t fill that role, they are like salt without flavor—useless and trampled.

f.w: salt that has lost its savor

chapters.n: But God has decreed the scattered Saints will return and rebuild Zion’s ruins.
After much tribulation comes the blessing, as promised before.
That blessing is redemption: restoration to Zion, never again to be thrown down.
But if they pollute their inheritances, they will be thrown down; God won’t spare them.
Zion’s redemption must come by power.
God will raise up a leader like Moses for his people.
They are Israel and Abraham’s seed, and must be delivered by God’s outstretched arm.
Zion’s redemption will follow the pattern of Israel’s exodus.
Don’t lose heart—unlike ancient Israel, who was told only an angel would go before them, not God’s presence.

f.w: Mine angel shall go up before you, but not my presence

chapters.n: Here both angels and God’s presence will go before them, and in time they will possess the good land.

f.w: Mine angels shall go up before you

chapters.n: Joseph Smith is the servant in the parable of the nobleman told to gather the strength of the house.

f.w: the parable which I have given unto you

chapters.n: Joseph is to call the young and middle-aged men to gather in Zion on land bought with consecrated money. This led to Zion’s Camp in 1834.

f.g: About 200 men eventually marched to Missouri in what became known as Zion’s Camp.

chapters.n: All branches should send wise men with money to buy land as commanded.
If enemies come to drive them off after these witnesses have been presented to God, they may curse them.
Whomever they curse, God will curse; they will avenge him.

f.w: whomsoever ye curse, I will curse

chapters.n: His presence will be with them, even to the third and fourth generation of those who hate him.
No one should fear dying for Christ; those who give their lives for him will find life.
Whoever is unwilling to lay down his life for him is not his disciple.
Sidney Rigdon is to preach in the East, preparing branches to keep the commandments about Zion’s redemption.
Parley P. Pratt and Lyman Wight should recruit companies—by tens, twenties, fifties, or hundreds—up to 500 men before returning.

f.w: by tens, or by twenties, or by fifties

chapters.n: This is God’s will—ask and receive—but people don’t always do it.
If not 500, then seek 300.

f.g: Perhaps.

chapters.n: If not 300, then 100.
They must not go up to Zion with fewer than 100 men.
Pray earnestly that Joseph may go with them, preside, organize the kingdom, and establish Zion on God’s laws.
All victory and glory come through diligence, faithfulness, and prayer.
Parley P. Pratt should travel with Joseph to recruit.
Lyman Wight with Sidney Rigdon.

f.g: An early convert and leader in Missouri; later an apostle.

chapters.n: Hyrum Smith with Frederick G. Williams.
Orson Hyde with Orson Pratt, as Joseph directs; the rest is left to the Lord.

f.w: leave the residue in my hands

chapters.n: The United Firm (the “united order”) had fallen into debt and dissension, especially after the Missouri losses. The Lord gives counsel about its properties; the order was meant to bless the Church and humanity until he comes.

f.g: The United Firm, a group of Church leaders who managed publishing and mercantile operations in Ohio and Missouri.

chapters.n: He had promised unchanging blessings to its faithful members.

f.g: A great number.

chapters.n: The unfaithful came near to being cursed.

f.g: Near.

chapters.n: Some members broke the covenant through greed and insincere words, and have been cursed.

f.g: False, insincere words.
Greed.

chapters.n: Anyone in the order who breaks the covenant will be cursed in this life and trodden down.
God is not to be mocked in these matters.
This protects the innocent from being condemned with the guilty, and ensures the guilty don’t escape. The faithful are promised a crown of glory.
Transgressors cannot escape God’s wrath in this life.
Those cut off for transgression will suffer the buffetings of Satan until the day of redemption.

f.g: Being left exposed to Satan’s attacks without God’s protection.

chapters.n: The order is given power to deliver unrepentant transgressors to Satan’s buffetings, so they can’t harm the faithful.
Members are to organize and each be assigned a personal stewardship.

f.g: Property or responsibility managed on behalf of the true owner, God.

chapters.n: Each will account to God for that stewardship.
God makes everyone accountable as stewards over the earthly blessings he created.
God stretched out the heavens and built the earth; everything in it is his.
He intends to provide for his Saints, since all things are his.
But it must be done his way: the poor are lifted up as the rich are humbled.

f.w: the poor shall be exalted, in that the rich are made low

chapters.n: A famous assurance: the earth is full, with enough and to spare. God gave people agency to manage it.
Whoever takes of God’s abundance but won’t share with the poor will, like the rich man in Jesus’s parable, lift up his eyes in torment.

f.w: lift up his eyes in hell, being in torment

f.g: Share, give.

chapters.n: Now specific stewardships of the order’s properties are assigned.
Sidney Rigdon receives his home and the tannery lot, to support him while he serves.

f.g: A workshop where animal hides are made into leather.

chapters.n: Everything is to be done by the order’s counsel and united vote in Kirtland.
This stewardship blesses Sidney and his descendants.

f.g: Descendants.

chapters.n: Blessings will multiply as long as he stays humble.
Martin Harris receives land John Johnson had obtained in exchange.

f.g: One of the Three Witnesses; he mortgaged his farm to pay for printing the Book of Mormon.

chapters.n: If faithful, he and his descendants will be blessed.
Martin is to use his money to spread the Lord’s word as Joseph directs.
Frederick G. Williams receives the place where he lives.
Oliver Cowdery receives the lot next to the planned printing office, plus the lot where his father lives.
Frederick G. Williams and Oliver Cowdery jointly receive the printing office.

f.g: Where Church newspapers and the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants were printed.

chapters.n: This is their stewardship.
If faithful, they will be blessed abundantly.
This is only the beginning of their stewardship, extending to their descendants.
Faithfulness brings a multitude of blessings to them and their children.
John Johnson receives his house and land, except ground reserved for the Lord’s houses and lots assigned to Oliver.
He will be blessed if faithful.
He should sell building lots for the Saints’ city as the Spirit and the order direct.

f.w: by the voice of the Spirit

chapters.n: This begins his stewardship, a blessing for his family.
Faithfulness brings many blessings.
Bishop Newel K. Whitney receives his home, the store and its lot, the corner lot, and the ashery.

f.g: A store; Whitney’s store in Kirtland housed the School of the Prophets.
A facility that made potash and soap from wood ashes—an important frontier industry.

chapters.n: These are his stewardship, for the benefit of the order’s store in the Kirtland stake.
The entire store operation is his stewardship, with his agent and descendants.
If faithful, he will be greatly blessed.
Joseph Smith receives the temple lot (40 by 12 rods) and the farm where his father lives.

f.g: A rod is 16.5 feet (about 5 meters); this lot was roughly 660 by 198 feet.

chapters.n: This begins his stewardship, blessing him and his father.
Joseph Sr.’s support is included in Joseph Jr.’s household.

f.g: Counted, considered.

chapters.n: Joseph’s household will be blessed as he is faithful.
The Kirtland and Missouri branches of the order are to separate.

f.g: Only in this way.

chapters.n: Kirtland’s group will be the “United Order of the Stake of Zion, the City of Kirtland”; Missouri’s, the “United Order of the City of Zion.”
Each will be organized and do business in its own name.
Kirtland’s group likewise conducts its own business.
This is for the salvation of both, given the Missouri expulsion and what is to come.
The covenants had been broken by greed and deceit.
So the two groups are dissolved, connected only by loans as circumstances allow and the council directs.

f.g: Formally ended as a joint organization.

chapters.n: More instruction about their stewardships follows.
All these properties belong to God; otherwise their faith is empty and their covenants broken.
If the properties are his, they are stewards; if not, they aren’t.
God has made them true stewards over his house.
Their main purpose: to print God’s words—scriptures and revelations, past and future.

f.g: Probably includes Joseph Smith’s Bible revision.

chapters.n: To build the Church and prepare people for the Lord’s coming, which is near.

f.w: when I shall dwell with them

chapters.n: They are to prepare and consecrate a treasury.

f.g: A place where money is safely kept.

chapters.n: Appoint and ordain a treasurer.
The treasury is sealed; sacred things go there, and no one may call any part his own—it belongs to all together.
From now on they should use their stewardships, apart from the sacred things, to print those sacred things.

f.g: An old expression meaning “get going.”

chapters.n: Proceeds from sacred things stay sealed in the treasury, used only by the order’s vote or by God’s command.

f.g: Proceeds, income.

chapters.n: These proceeds are preserved for sacred and holy purposes.
It will be called the sacred treasury of the Lord.
A second, general treasury is also to be set up with its own treasurer and seal.
All money earned from improving their stewardships—houses, land, cattle, anything but sacred writings—goes into this treasury as it comes in.
Whether five dollars or a hundred, it goes in.
No one may call it his own.
Nothing may be withdrawn except by the order’s common consent.
Common consent works like this: a member tells the treasurer, “I need this for my stewardship.”
And the treasurer gives what is requested, whatever the amount.
Unless the member is shown before the council to be an unfaithful or unwise steward.

f.w: an unfaithful and an unwise steward

chapters.n: While faithful and in fellowship, his request is his token and must not be refused. The system rests on trust.

f.g: Sign, proof of authorization.

chapters.n: If there is transgression, the treasurer follows the council’s direction.
If the treasurer himself proves unfaithful, the council removes and replaces him.

f.g: In his place.

chapters.n: About debts: God wants them to pay all their debts.
They must humble themselves and obtain this blessing through diligence, humility, and prayer.
If they do, God will soften creditors’ hearts until he provides means for their deliverance.
They should write promptly to creditors in New York as the Spirit directs, and God will soften those creditors.

f.g: Much of the Kirtland store’s merchandise had been purchased on credit from New York merchants.

chapters.n: If humble and faithful, they will have victory.
God promises to deliver them from this debt “this once.”

f.g: Here, the burden of debt.

chapters.n: They may borrow in hundreds or thousands if needed to free themselves.

f.g: Here, to borrow.

chapters.n: They may pledge the properties as collateral this one time, by common consent.

f.g: Offer as security for a loan.

chapters.n: This permission is for this once. If they obey, everything remains God’s, they are his stewards, and he won’t let his house be broken up.

f.w: the master will not suffer his house to be broken up

chapters.n: Zion’s Camp—about two hundred volunteers who marched from Ohio—was camped near Fishing River in Clay County, Missouri. The Lord speaks to those gathered to learn his will about redeeming his afflicted people.

f.g: Given on June 22, 1834, at Fishing River, Missouri.

chapters.n: If not for the Church’s transgressions as a whole (not every individual), Zion might have been redeemed already.

f.w: concerning the church and not individuals
f.g: A collective, not a personal, judgment.

chapters.n: They hadn’t learned obedience, were full of wrongdoing, and didn’t share with the poor as Saints should.
They weren’t united as the celestial law requires.

f.w: the law of the celestial kingdom

chapters.n: Zion can only be built on celestial principles; otherwise God can’t receive her.
So his people must be corrected until they learn obedience—even through suffering, as Christ himself learned.
This doesn’t apply to all the first elders who lead; not all are under condemnation.
It applies to the outlying branches, many of whom said they’d only go to Zion and give money if God first proved he’d deliver them.
So the elders must wait “a little season” for Zion’s redemption.
So they can be prepared, and the people better taught and experienced in their duties.
That can’t happen until the elders are endowed with power from on high.

f.w: endowed with power from on high

chapters.n: God has prepared a great endowment to pour out on the faithful and humble. It was fulfilled in part at the Kirtland Temple in 1836.
So the elders should wait for Zion’s redemption.
God does not require them to fight Zion’s battles; as promised, he will fight for them.
The destroyer has gone forth against his enemies; within a few years they won’t pollute his land.

f.g: Inheritance; God’s chosen land or people.

chapters.n: God had told Joseph to call the strength of his house to redeem Zion.

f.w: throw down the towers of mine enemies

chapters.n: But most of the strength of his house didn’t respond.

f.g: Far fewer than the hoped-for 500 men volunteered.

chapters.n: For those who did obey, he has prepared a blessing and endowment if they remain faithful.
He accepts their offering; they were brought this far as a test of faith. Many future leaders, including most of the first Twelve Apostles, came from Zion’s Camp.
Those who can stay in the area should stay.
Those with families in the East may return for a while as Joseph directs.
God will counsel Joseph, and his appointments will be fulfilled.
Saints in the area should be faithful, prayerful, and humble, and keep these revelations private until it’s wise to share them.
Don’t talk of judgments or boast of faith or miracles; gather carefully in one region as local feelings allow.
God will give them favor with their neighbors so they can live peacefully while seeking legal justice.
This way they’ll find favor until the “army of Israel” grows very great.

f.g: The body of faithful Saints, prepared and sanctified.

chapters.n: God will soften hearts, as he dealt with Pharaoh from time to time, giving Joseph and the elders time to gather strength.

f.w: as I did the heart of Pharaoh

chapters.n: And to send wise men to buy all available land in Jackson and surrounding counties.
God wants these lands bought and then held under the law of consecration.
Once purchased, Israel would be guiltless in taking possession of their own lands and defending them.
But first the army must grow and be sanctified—fair as the sun, clear as the moon, with banners that inspire awe.

f.w: fair as the sun, and clear as the moon

f.g: Awe-inspiring.

chapters.n: So that worldly kingdoms will acknowledge Zion as the kingdom of God and his Christ.

f.w: the kingdom of our God and his Christ

chapters.n: The first elders should receive their endowment in the house being built in Kirtland.

f.g: The Kirtland Temple, dedicated March 27, 1836.

chapters.n: Zion’s laws are to be carried out after her redemption.
There has been a day of calling; now comes a day of choosing. The worthy will be chosen.
The Spirit will show Joseph who is chosen, and they will be sanctified.
If they follow counsel, they will eventually have power to accomplish everything for Zion.
Seek peace—not only with those who attacked them but with all people.

f.g: Earnestly seek peace.

chapters.n: Raise a banner of peace and proclaim peace to the ends of the earth.

f.g: A flag or symbol of peace.

chapters.n: Offer peace to those who struck them, as the Spirit directs, and all things will work for their good.

f.w: all things shall work together for your good

chapters.n: So be faithful—Christ is with them to the end.

f.w: I am with you even unto the end

chapters.n: Warren A. Cowdery, Oliver Cowdery’s older brother, is called as presiding high priest over the Saints in and around Freedom, New York.

f.g: Older brother of Oliver Cowdery; he later served as a Church clerk and scribe in Kirtland.
A town in western New York.

chapters.n: He is to preach the gospel and warn people, both locally and in neighboring counties.
He should devote his whole time to this sacred calling, seeking God’s kingdom first; what he needs will be provided, for a laborer deserves his support.

f.w: seeking diligently the kingdom of heaven
the laborer is worthy of his hire

chapters.n: The Lord’s coming is near and will surprise the world like a thief at night.

f.w: as a thief in the night

f.g: Comes near.

chapters.n: So prepare—“gird up your loins”—to be children of light, and that day won’t catch you unprepared.

f.g: Tie up long robes to be ready for action; be prepared.

chapters.n: Heaven rejoiced when Warren submitted to God’s rule and left behind worldly schemes.

f.g: Submitted to the Lord’s authority.
Human cunning or worldly practices.

chapters.n: He is blessed, and God will have mercy. Despite the pride of his heart, God will lift him up if he humbles himself.

f.g: Pride, self-importance.

chapters.n: God will give him grace and confidence to stand; if he stays a faithful witness and light to the Church, a crown awaits him in the Father’s mansions.

This major revelation on priesthood combines material from March 1835 with an earlier 1831 revelation (verses 59–100 draw on it). It begins: the Church has two priesthoods, the Melchizedek and the Aaronic, which includes the Levitical.

f.g: The priesthood given to the tribe of Levi in ancient Israel; part of the Aaronic.

chapters.n: The higher priesthood is named after Melchizedek because he was such a great high priest.
Its full name is the Holy Priesthood after the Order of the Son of God.

f.w: the Order of the Son of God

chapters.n: Out of reverence, to avoid repeating God’s name too often, ancient believers called it after Melchizedek.

f.g: God.

chapters.n: All other offices in the Church are “appendages” of the Melchizedek Priesthood.

f.g: Parts that branch from a larger whole.

chapters.n: Yet there are two main divisions: Melchizedek and Aaronic (or Levitical).
The office of elder belongs to the Melchizedek Priesthood.
The Melchizedek Priesthood holds the right to preside and authority over all Church offices in every age, for spiritual matters.

f.g: The authority to lead and direct.

chapters.n: The First Presidency may officiate in every Church office.

f.w: The Presidency of the High Priesthood

chapters.n: High priests may officiate in their own office under the Presidency and also as elders, priests, teachers, deacons, and members.

f.g: In their own office or rank.

chapters.n: An elder may act in place of a high priest who isn’t present.

f.g: In his place.

chapters.n: High priests and elders administer spiritual things and may fill all these offices when no higher authority is present.
The second priesthood is named after Aaron, Moses’s brother, because it was given to him and his descendants.
It is called “lesser” because it is attached to the greater priesthood and has power over outward ordinances like baptism and the sacrament.

f.g: Visible ceremonies such as baptism and the sacrament.

chapters.n: The bishopric presides over the Aaronic Priesthood and holds its keys.

f.g: A bishop and his counselors.

chapters.n: Only a literal descendant of Aaron has a legal right to this office by birth.
But a high priest may serve as bishop when no such descendant is available, if called and set apart by the First Presidency. This is how bishops are called today.

f.g: Formally given authority to serve in a specific calling by the laying on of hands.

chapters.n: The Melchizedek Priesthood holds the keys of all the Church’s spiritual blessings.

f.w: the keys of all the spiritual blessings

chapters.n: Its holders may receive the mysteries of heaven, see the heavens opened, and commune with the Church of the Firstborn and with God the Father and Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant.

f.w: the general assembly and church of the Firstborn
Jesus the mediator of the new covenant

chapters.n: The Aaronic Priesthood holds the keys of the ministering of angels and administers outward ordinances and baptism for remission of sins.

f.w: the keys of the ministering of angels

f.g: The outward, foundational practices of the gospel.

chapters.n: Presidents or presiding officers naturally arise from among those ordained to each office.
Three presiding high priests, chosen, ordained, and sustained by the Church’s faith and prayers, form the First Presidency quorum.
The Twelve Apostles are traveling councilors and special witnesses of Christ’s name to all the world. The first Twelve of this dispensation were called in February 1835.

f.w: special witnesses of the name of Christ

chapters.n: Their quorum is equal in authority to the First Presidency.

f.g: Equal as a body when the First Presidency is dissolved (as at a prophet’s death); otherwise the Twelve work under the Presidency’s direction.

chapters.n: The Seventy are also called to preach and are special witnesses to the Gentiles and the world.
Their quorum is equal in authority to the Twelve.
Decisions of these quorums must be unanimous to have full validity.

f.g: Every member agrees.

chapters.n: A majority may act as a quorum when necessary.
Otherwise their decisions won’t carry the blessings that came to ancient presiding quorums of righteous men.
Decisions must be made with righteousness, holiness, humility, meekness, patience, faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, godliness, kindness, and charity.

f.g: Patient endurance.
Self-control.

chapters.n: For if these qualities abound, they won’t be unfruitful in knowing the Lord.
An unrighteous decision may be brought before a general assembly of the quorums; otherwise there’s no appeal.
The Twelve are a traveling presiding high council under the First Presidency, building and regulating the Church among all nations—first Gentiles, then Jews.

f.w: first unto the Gentiles and secondly unto the Jews

chapters.n: The Seventy work under the Twelve’s direction in the same mission.
The Twelve hold the keys to open the door to the gospel among the nations.
Stake high councils are equal in authority, in their local affairs, to the Presidency or the Twelve.
The high council in Zion is equal in authority to the Twelve’s councils at the stakes.
The Twelve should call on the Seventy, rather than others, when they need help preaching.
The Twelve are to ordain “evangelical ministers”—patriarchs—in large branches as revealed.

f.g: Patriarchs, who give special blessings to Church members.

chapters.n: This patriarchal order was to pass from father to son among the chosen lineage.

f.w: handed down from father to son

chapters.n: It began with Adam and came down by lineage as follows.
Adam ordained Seth at 69 and later promised that Seth’s descendants would be chosen and preserved to the earth’s end.

f.g: Descendants.

chapters.n: Seth was a perfect man who looked exactly like his father, distinguishable only by age.

f.g: Exact image.

chapters.n: Adam ordained Enos at age 134 years and four months.
God called Cainan at 40; he met Adam on the way to Shedolamak and was ordained at 87.

f.g: A place named only here.

chapters.n: Adam ordained and blessed Mahalaleel at 496 years and seven days.
Adam ordained and blessed Jared at 200.
Enoch was ordained by Adam at 25 and blessed by him at 65.
Enoch saw the Lord and walked with God 365 years; he was 430 when he and his city were taken to heaven.

f.g: Changed so as not to experience death, and taken up.

chapters.n: Adam ordained Methuselah at 100.
Seth ordained Lamech at 32.

f.g: Noah’s father, not the Lamech of Cain’s line.

chapters.n: Methuselah ordained Noah at 10.
Three years before his death, Adam gathered his righteous high-priest descendants in the valley of Adam-ondi-Ahman and gave them his final blessing.

f.g: A place in Missouri where Adam blessed his posterity.

chapters.n: The Lord appeared, and they blessed Adam, calling him Michael, the prince, the archangel.
The Lord comforted Adam: he is set at the head, nations will come from him, and he is their prince forever.
Though bent with age, Adam stood full of the Holy Ghost and prophesied all that would happen to his descendants.

f.g: Adam lived 930 years.

chapters.n: This was recorded in the book of Enoch, to be made known in due time.

f.g: Not the same as the ancient “1 Enoch” known today; a record still to be revealed.

chapters.n: The Twelve are also to ordain and organize all other Church officers, according to the following revelation.
The following verses come from a November 1831 revelation addressed to the Church in Zion.
Presiding elders must preside over elders.

f.g: Lord of armies—God as commander of heaven’s forces.

chapters.n: Priests must preside over priests.
And likewise teachers over teachers, and deacons over deacons.
Each office has its order—deacon, teacher, priest, elder—according to the Church’s covenants.

f.g: Each separately.

chapters.n: Then comes the High Priesthood, the greatest of all.
One must be appointed as President of the High Priesthood of the Church.

f.g: Joseph Smith was sustained to this office in January 1832.

chapters.n: In other words, the Presiding High Priest over the High Priesthood.
From this priesthood come ordinances and blessings by the laying on of hands.
A bishop’s office is not equal to it, because a bishop administers temporal (material) things.

f.g: Practical, material matters like property and care of the poor.

chapters.n: A bishop must be a high priest unless he is a literal descendant of Aaron.
Only a literal descendant of Aaron holds those keys by birthright.
Still, a high priest may be set apart to manage temporal things, guided by the Spirit of truth.
He is also a “judge in Israel,” handling Church business and judging transgressors with his counselors.
This is the duty of a bishop who is a high priest rather than a descendant of Aaron.
He will be a common judge in Zion, a stake, or a branch, until Zion grows and more bishops are needed.
Other bishops serve in the same office.
A literal descendant of Aaron may preside without counselors, except when a President of the High Priesthood is on trial.
Decisions of these councils follow this commandment.
The most important and difficult cases, if unresolved by bishops, go to the council of the Church before the First Presidency.
The Presidency may call twelve high priests as counselors and decide cases on testimony.
Their decision is final; it is the highest council of the Church on spiritual controversies.

f.g: Considered settled; not to be raised again.

chapters.n: No Church member is exempt from this council.
Even a President of the High Priesthood who transgresses is accountable before a council with twelve high priest counselors.

f.g: A council made up of the bishop and counselors; see D&C 107:76.

chapters.n: Their decision about him ends the matter.
No one is above God’s justice and law; all is done in order and solemnity.
A deacons quorum president presides over twelve deacons, counsels with them, and teaches them their duties.

f.g: A quorum of up to twelve deacons, still the pattern today.

chapters.n: A teachers quorum president presides over up to twenty-four teachers.
A priests quorum president presides over up to forty-eight priests.
That president is the bishop—one of the duties of his office.
An elders quorum president presides over up to ninety-six elders.
This quorum is distinct from the Seventy and is for those who don’t travel worldwide.
The President of the High Priesthood presides over the whole Church and is to be like Moses.
He is a seer, revelator, translator, and prophet, with all the gifts God gives the head of the Church.

f.w: a seer, a revelator, a translator, and a prophet

chapters.n: As shown in a vision, the Seventy are to have seven presidents chosen from among them.
The seventh of these presidents presides over the other six.
These presidents choose additional Seventies beyond the first and preside over them.
And so on, up to seven times seventy, if the work requires it.

f.g: The Lord’s field of labor, the world.

chapters.n: The Seventy are traveling ministers to the Gentiles first and also to the Jews.
Other officers don’t have the obligation to travel to all nations, though they may hold high and responsible offices.
A famous charge: let every man learn his duty and act in his office with all diligence.

f.w: let every man learn his duty

chapters.n: The lazy, and those who don’t learn their duty and prove themselves, won’t be counted worthy to stand.

f.g: Lazy.

chapters.n: Lyman Sherman, a member of the Seventy, came to Joseph Smith asking for the Lord’s word. The Lord forgives his sins because he obeyed the prompting to come and seek counsel from the prophet.

f.g: Lyman R. Sherman, one of the first presidents of the Seventy.

chapters.n: He can be at peace about his standing before God—and should stop resisting the Lord’s voice.

f.w: let your soul be at rest

chapters.n: He should be more careful to keep his vows, and he will receive great blessings.

f.g: Solemn promises or covenants made to God.

chapters.n: He should wait patiently for the solemn assembly, when he will be remembered with the first elders and ordained with them.

f.g: Held in the Kirtland Temple in March 1836.

chapters.n: This is the Father’s promise, if he stays faithful.
From that day he will have authority to preach wherever the Lord sends him.
So he should strengthen his brethren in everything—his conversation, prayers, encouragement, and actions.

f.g: In older English, one’s whole manner of life and conduct, not just speech.
Words of encouragement and urging.

chapters.n: The Lord is with him to bless and deliver him forever.

Joseph Smith begins the dedicatory prayer of the Kirtland Temple on March 27, 1836, with thanks. He praises God as the One who keeps his promises and shows mercy to those who serve him wholeheartedly. The prayer had been given to Joseph by revelation and was read aloud to the congregation.
The Saints built this temple because God commanded it. Kirtland, Ohio, was the Church’s headquarters at the time, and the temple was its first in this dispensation.

f.w: build a house to thy name

chapters.n: A simple report of obedience: the Lord asked for a house, and his people built it. Like Solomon at the dedication of his temple, Joseph presents the finished work to God.

The prayer is offered to the Father in the name of Jesus Christ, the only name through which salvation comes. Joseph asks God to accept the building as the Saints’ own handiwork, offered at his request.

f.w: in whose name alone salvation can be administered

chapters.n: The temple cost the poor Saints dearly—men labored on it while others were driven from Missouri, and families gave what little they had. Its purpose was to be a place where the Savior could reveal himself, which he did a week later.

f.g: The temple took about three years (1833–1836) and drained the Church’s resources during a time of poverty and persecution.

f.w: that the Son of Man might have a place to manifest himself

chapters.n: Joseph quotes from an earlier revelation (D&C 88) in which the Lord called these men his friends and commanded a “solemn assembly”—a sacred gathering of the priesthood.

Still quoting D&C 88, this verse gives a famous charge: since not everyone has strong faith, the Saints must teach each other and learn from the best books—gaining knowledge through both study and faith.

f.w: seek learning even by study and also by faith

chapters.n: The Lord’s list of what his house should be: prayer, fasting, faith, learning, glory, order, and God. This description, from D&C 88:119, still shapes how Latter-day Saints view temples and even their homes.
All coming and going, and every greeting, should be done in the Lord’s name. Raised hands were a gesture of worship and covenant in the early Church.

f.g: Entering and leaving; the whole of one’s comings and goings.

chapters.n: Joseph asks God’s grace to help the Saints hold their solemn assembly in a way that honors him and that he will accept.

f.g: Here, divine help and enabling power given freely by God.

chapters.n: The Saints want to be worthy to receive what God had promised them—especially an “endowment” of spiritual power from on high.

f.w: the promises which thou hast made

chapters.n: The heart of the dedication: Joseph asks that God’s glory rest on the people and the building, that it be made holy, and that the Lord’s presence remain there continually.

f.w: which we now dedicate to thee
f.g: To dedicate is to formally set something apart for God’s exclusive, sacred use.

chapters.n: Joseph prays that anyone who simply steps through the door will feel God’s power and recognize the temple as a holy place.

f.g: The doorway or entrance of a building.

chapters.n: The temple was also a school. Joseph asks that those who worship there will learn wisdom from the best books, through study and through faith, as the Lord commanded.

f.w: words of wisdom out of the best books

chapters.n: Joseph prays that worshippers will grow spiritually, receive the full gift of the Holy Ghost, and be organized according to God’s laws.
The list from verse 8 returns as a prayer: may this truly be a house of prayer, fasting, faith, glory, and God—“even thy house.”

f.w: a house of prayer, a house of fasting

chapters.n: Echoing the Lord’s words, Joseph asks that every entrance into the temple be done in the Lord’s name—with the right purpose and spirit.

f.w: in the name of the Lord

chapters.n: Likewise, every departure from the temple should be in the Lord’s name, so that what people receive inside goes with them into the world.

f.g: Departures; going out.

chapters.n: Greetings, too, should be holy. “Holy hands” echo Paul’s counsel that people pray lifting up clean, sincere hands.
The temple must be protected from anything impure. This principle still guides who may enter dedicated temples today.

Joseph acknowledges that the Saints will make mistakes. He prays that when they do, they will repent quickly and be restored to the temple’s blessings. The temple is a place of mercy as well as holiness.
Joseph prays that missionaries will go out from the temple filled with God’s power, carrying his name, surrounded by his glory, and guarded by angels. This is the “endowment” the Lord had promised.

f.w: thine angels have charge over them

chapters.n: From Kirtland, the good news would spread worldwide, showing that God was fulfilling ancient prophecies about the last days.

f.w: unto the ends of the earth

chapters.n: Joseph asks God to make the temple worshippers a stable, honorable people for all generations and for eternity.

f.w: to all generations and for eternity

chapters.n: Borrowing Isaiah and the Psalms, Joseph asks that weapons against the Saints fail and that those who scheme against them be caught in their own traps.

f.w: no weapon formed against them shall prosper
he who diggeth a pit for them shall fall into the same himself

chapters.n: Joseph prays that no organized conspiracy of evil will overpower the people who bear God’s name.

f.g: An organized group united for evil; compare the “secret combinations” of the Book of Mormon.

chapters.n: Here and in the next verse, Joseph asks God to defend his people against attackers. Persecution in Missouri was fresh in everyone’s memory.
Joseph recalls how God fought for Israel in ancient battles and asks him to deliver the Saints in the same way.

f.w: as thou didst in the day of battle

chapters.n: Joseph asks that those spreading lies about the Church be confounded—but only “if they will not repent” after hearing the gospel. Even his pleas for justice leave room for mercy.

f.g: Slanderous rumors and newspaper stories that circulated widely against Joseph Smith and the Saints.

chapters.n: He prays that God’s judgments will sweep away the work of slanderers, so that the lies against his people will finally end.
Joseph affirms that the Saints suffered not for wrongdoing but for testifying of God.
A plea for complete relief from oppression, pictured as a heavy yoke on the shoulders of a work animal.

f.g: A wooden frame binding oxen together; a common scriptural image for bondage or burden.

chapters.n: “Break it off”—the repetition expresses deep feeling. The Saints want freedom so they can rise up and do God’s work in their generation.
Joseph addresses God as Jehovah, asking him to forgive the people’s sins and blot them out forever. All people sin; all need mercy.

f.g: In Latter-day Saint understanding, Jehovah is the premortal name of Jesus Christ; in this prayer the title is also used in addressing God.

f.w: let them be blotted out forever

chapters.n: Priesthood leaders had received anointings in the temple in the weeks before the dedication. Joseph asks that these anointings be confirmed with power from heaven.

f.g: In early 1836, leaders were ceremonially anointed with oil in the Kirtland Temple in preparation for the promised endowment.

chapters.n: Joseph asks for a new Pentecost—the gift of tongues and “cloven tongues as of fire.” Many attendees reported such experiences during the dedication season.
He prays that the temple will be filled with God’s glory like a rushing mighty wind. Witnesses that evening reported hearing such a sound and seeing light around the temple.
Joseph prays that missionaries will carry a covenant witness that seals their testimony and prepares Saints for coming judgments, so they will not lose courage in hard times.

f.g: Lose heart; give up from fear or weakness.

chapters.n: Where people accept the gospel, Joseph asks for peace and salvation on that city, and that the righteous gather to Zion and its stakes with joyful songs.

f.g: From Isaiah’s image of tent pegs that hold up Zion’s tent; an organized area of the Church.

chapters.n: Joseph asks God to hold back judgment from such a city until its righteous people have been gathered out, as Lot was rescued before Sodom’s fall.

f.w: let not thy judgments fall upon that city

chapters.n: But cities that reject the warning must face what the prophets foretold. “Untoward” means crooked or rebellious.

f.g: Untoward = perverse, stubborn.

chapters.n: Joseph asks God to protect missionaries and to cleanse them “from their blood”—that is, free them of responsibility for those who heard and rejected their warning.
A tender line: the Saints take no pleasure in anyone’s destruction. Every soul is precious to God.

f.w: their souls are precious before thee

chapters.n: Yet God’s word must be fulfilled. Like the Savior in Gethsemane, they pray for grace to say, “Thy will be done.”

f.w: Thy will be done, O Lord, and not ours

chapters.n: Prophets have foretold terrible judgments on the wicked in the last days. Joseph acknowledges these warnings soberly.

f.w: pour out thy judgments, without measure

chapters.n: He asks God to spare his people from the calamity coming on the wicked and to prepare his servants for “the day of burning”—the Second Coming.
Joseph now prays for the Saints expelled from Jackson County, Missouri, in 1833, who lost homes and land meant to be their inheritance in Zion.

f.w: driven by the inhabitants of Jackson county, Missouri

chapters.n: The Saints in Kirtland grieve for their brothers and sisters still suffering in Missouri.

f.w: our hearts flow out with sorrow

chapters.n: “How long?”—the cry of the Psalms. Joseph asks how long innocent suffering must continue before God acts.

f.g: Allow, permit.

chapters.n: Strikingly, Joseph first asks for mercy on the mob, praying they will stop plundering and repent. This reflects Jesus’ command to pray for enemies.

f.g: To plunder or rob.

f.w: Have mercy, O Lord, upon the wicked mob

chapters.n: If they will not repent, Joseph asks God to “make bare his arm”—show his power openly—and redeem the land appointed for Zion.
Only if there is no other way, he asks for judgment so that God’s cause will not fail. “Root and branch” means completely.
But if they repent, God will turn away his anger as he looks on “the face of thine Anointed”—Jesus Christ, whose atonement makes mercy possible.

f.g: Hebrew Messiah and Greek Christ both mean “anointed one.”

chapters.n: Joseph prays for all nations and for American rulers, and asks that the principles of the U.S. Constitution be established forever. The Saints relied on its protections of religious freedom.
The prayer widens to the whole world: kings and princes, churches of every kind, and the poor, needy, and afflicted.

f.w: the poor, the needy, and afflicted ones

chapters.n: He asks that people’s hearts soften and their prejudices give way to truth when missionaries come, so God’s people may find favor.

f.w: prejudices may give way before the truth
f.g: Prejudice = judging before knowing. Missionaries often met opinions formed from rumors.

chapters.n: The goal: that the whole earth may know that these servants have heard God’s voice and were truly sent by him.
The “sons of Jacob”—members of covenant Israel—are to gather the righteous from all nations to build a holy city, Zion.

f.w: build a holy city to thy name

chapters.n: Joseph asks God to designate more stakes beyond Kirtland so the gathering could grow. “Cut short in righteousness” means that God will finish his work swiftly.
The Saints describe themselves as “identified with the Gentiles”—they came mostly from non-Israelite nations, even though the gospel would make them part of covenant Israel.
Yet God loves the descendants of Jacob, who have long been scattered “upon the mountains … in a cloudy and dark day,” as Ezekiel described.
Joseph prays for mercy on Israel and that Jerusalem’s redemption may begin “from this hour.” Five years later Orson Hyde dedicated the Holy Land for the return of the Jews.

f.w: Jerusalem, from this hour, may begin to be redeemed

chapters.n: The house of David—the Jewish people and their royal line—has long been under a yoke of bondage. Joseph prays it will begin to be lifted.
He asks that the Jews begin returning to the land promised to their father Abraham.

f.w: the lands which thou didst give to Abraham

chapters.n: Joseph prays for the “remnants of Jacob”—understood by the early Saints as Native Americans descended from Book of Mormon peoples—to receive the fulness of the gospel. The language reflects 1830s attitudes; the hope expressed is for their spiritual blessing.
He hopes they will lay down weapons and end conflict—echoing Book of Mormon stories of converted peoples burying their weapons.

f.w: lay down their weapons of bloodshed

chapters.n: Finally, all scattered Israel should come to know the truth, believe in the Messiah, be freed from oppression, and rejoice before God.
Joseph humbly asks God to remember him—his trials, his covenants, and his sincere efforts to obey. Prophets need prayers too.
He prays for Emma and their children, that they will be preserved by God’s “fostering” (nurturing) hand and exalted.

f.g: Emma Smith and their children; at the time this included young Joseph Smith III and the adopted Julia Murdock Smith.

chapters.n: Joseph prays for his extended family and Emma’s relatives, some of whom opposed his work, asking that their prejudices be washed away and that they be converted.

f.g: Close relatives, especially in-laws. Emma’s father, Isaac Hale, strongly opposed Joseph.

chapters.n: He prays for all the presidents of the Church and their families, that their names may be honored through the generations.
The prayer embraces the entire Church—families, sick, poor, and meek—and pleads that God’s kingdom will fill the earth as Daniel foresaw: a stone cut without hands that becomes a great mountain.
Borrowing from the Song of Solomon, the Church is pictured emerging from a dark wilderness, beautiful as the moon, clear as the sun, and awe-inspiring as a bannered army.

f.w: fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners

f.g: Awe-inspiring, formidable.

chapters.n: The Church is to be prepared like a bride for the Savior’s return, when the earth will be reshaped and filled with his glory.
At the trumpet that calls the dead to rise, the faithful will be caught up to meet the Lord and be with him forever.

f.w: caught up in the cloud to meet thee

chapters.n: Clean garments, robes of righteousness, palms, and crowns are images from Revelation for the redeemed who have overcome through Christ.
Joseph closes by addressing God enthroned in heaven, piling up attributes—glory, power, truth, justice, mercy—to express how far beyond words God is.
“O hear, O hear, O hear us”—a threefold plea of great intensity, asking God to answer and accept the house built to his name.

f.w: accept the dedication of this house

chapters.n: The Saints long to join their voices with the seraphs around God’s throne. After the prayer, the congregation gave the Hosanna Shout, still part of temple dedications today.

f.g: Hebrew seraphim, “burning ones”—angels around God’s throne.
Hebrew “save, we pray”; a shout of praise.

chapters.n: The prayer ends asking that the anointed be clothed with salvation and that the Saints shout for joy. The choir then sang “The Spirit of God,” written for this occasion.

On Easter Sunday, April 3, 1836, one week after the dedication, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery prayed behind curtains at the Melchizedek Priesthood pulpits. Spiritual eyes were opened, and they saw beyond the ordinary world.

f.w: The veil was taken from our minds

chapters.n: They saw the Lord standing on the front rail of the pulpit. The gold pavement beneath him recalls what Moses and the elders of Israel saw on Sinai.

f.g: The front ledge or railing of the raised pulpit.

f.w: a paved work of pure gold

f.g: A golden-yellow color.

chapters.n: The description closely parallels John’s vision of the risen Christ: flaming eyes, snow-white hair, a face brighter than the sun, a voice like rushing waters. The speaker is Jehovah—Jesus Christ.

f.w: His eyes were as a flame of fire

chapters.n: Christ identifies himself as the eternal, living One who was crucified—and as the one who pleads our case before the Father.

f.w: I am the first and the last

chapters.n: The first words to Joseph and Oliver are forgiveness and joy. Before keys are given, the Savior assures them they are clean.

f.w: lift up your heads and rejoice

chapters.n: The Lord invites all the Saints who sacrificed to build the temple to share in this joy.
Here is the direct answer to the dedicatory prayer: the Lord accepts the house and promises to reveal himself there in mercy.
The Lord promises to appear and speak to his servants—on condition that the people keep his commandments and keep the temple holy.

f.w: do not pollute this holy house

chapters.n: Countless people will rejoice because of the blessings and the “endowment” of power the Lord’s servants received in this temple.

f.g: A gift, especially of spiritual power; the Kirtland endowment was a preparatory outpouring before the fuller Nauvoo temple ordinances.

chapters.n: The temple’s fame will reach other lands, and this is only “the beginning” of blessings—pointing toward many temples to come.

f.g: Today Latter-day Saints have temples on every inhabited continent.

chapters.n: Next Moses appears. As the prophet who led Israel out of Egypt, he gives Joseph and Oliver the keys—the authority to direct—the gathering of scattered Israel, including the lost ten tribes.

f.w: the ten tribes from the land of the north

f.g: The right to direct and authorize the use of priesthood power for a particular work.

chapters.n: A messenger called Elias restores the “dispensation of the gospel of Abraham”—the covenant promises made to Abraham, including that through his seed all nations would be blessed.

f.g: Greek form of Elijah, but used in latter-day scripture as a title for a forerunner or restorer; this messenger’s identity is not otherwise specified.

f.w: in us and our seed all generations after us should be blessed

chapters.n: Then Elijah appears—the Old Testament prophet who was taken to heaven in a chariot of fire without dying.

f.w: taken to heaven without tasting death

chapters.n: Elijah announces that Malachi’s prophecy—that Elijah would come before the great day of the Lord—is now fulfilled. Many Jewish families set a place for Elijah at Passover; this appearance came during the Passover season of 1836.

f.w: spoken of by the mouth of Malachi

chapters.n: Elijah’s purpose is to bind families together across generations. Without these sealing ties, the earth would be “smitten with a curse”—God’s purpose for his children would fail.

f.w: turn the hearts of the fathers to the children

chapters.n: Elijah hands over the keys for this final dispensation—understood by Latter-day Saints as the sealing power that makes temple ordinances binding in heaven. His coming is a sign that the Second Coming is near.

In 1836 Joseph Smith, Hyrum Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Oliver Cowdery traveled to Salem, Massachusetts, partly hoping to find money to pay heavy Church debts. The Lord gently says he is not displeased, despite their “follies”—foolish choices.

f.g: Foolish actions or misjudgments.

chapters.n: The Lord points to a different kind of treasure: people in Salem who would later join the Church and strengthen Zion. Several years later, missionaries did baptize converts there.

f.g: Means or agency; acting as the Lord’s instrument.

chapters.n: They are to get to know people in the city, following the Spirit’s guidance.

f.g: Fitting, useful, wise.

chapters.n: The Lord promises that in time the city will be “given into their hands”—commonly understood as fulfilled through conversion and influence rather than wealth found on this trip. “Secret parts” likely refers to their private plans or vulnerabilities.

f.g: Probably hidden matters or weaknesses; the phrase echoes Isaiah 3:17. Its exact meaning here is uncertain.

chapters.n: The Lord tells them not to be anxious about their debts; he will give them ability to pay.

f.w: Concern not yourselves about your debts

chapters.n: Nor should they worry about Zion in Missouri; the Lord will be merciful to her.

f.w: I will deal mercifully with her

chapters.n: They are to stay in Salem and the surrounding area for a while.

f.g: Stay, remain.

chapters.n: The Lord will show them where to stay by the peace and power of his Spirit—a pattern for seeking guidance.

f.g: Made known by a sign; pointed out.

f.w: peace and power of my Spirit

chapters.n: They may rent lodging there. They are also to research the city’s early settlers and founders—some suggest this hints at family history, since Joseph’s ancestors lived nearby in Topsfield.

f.g: Rent.

f.w: more ancient inhabitants and founders of this city
f.g: Salem was founded in 1626; Joseph Smith’s Smith ancestors had lived in nearby Topsfield.

chapters.n: There is “more than one” kind of treasure here—hinting that the most important riches are not money.
The Lord closes with Jesus’ advice to be wise as serpents yet without sin, and promises to arrange all things for their good as fast as they can handle it.

f.w: order all things for your good

chapters.n: On July 23, 1837—the very day the first missionaries began preaching in England—the Lord speaks to Thomas B. Marsh, President of the Quorum of the Twelve. His prayers and generosity for his fellow apostles have been noticed.

f.w: thine alms have come up as a memorial before me

f.g: Gifts to the poor or needy; acts of charity.

chapters.n: Gently but honestly, the Lord notes some things in Thomas’s heart that displeased him—possibly feelings about being passed over when Heber C. Kimball and Orson Hyde were sent to England.

f.w: some few things in thine heart
f.g: Thomas was reportedly upset that Joseph sent apostles to England without consulting him as quorum president.

chapters.n: Because Thomas has humbled himself, he will be lifted up, and his sins are forgiven.

f.w: abased thyself thou shalt be exalted

f.g: Humbled, lowered.

chapters.n: The Lord encourages Thomas: he will testify to Gentiles and Jews and send God’s word to the ends of the earth through the Twelve’s missionary work.
Thomas is to labor constantly, warning people morning and evening, so that his message keeps people awake spiritually.

f.g: Strive, work earnestly.

chapters.n: He is to keep his home in Zion and not move away; the Lord has a great work for him.

f.g: Making known; proclaiming. Thomas was also involved in Church printing.

chapters.n: “Gird up thy loins” means get ready for action, as men tucked up long robes to run or work. Shod feet signal readiness to travel among mountains and nations.

f.g: Wearing shoes; ready to travel.

chapters.n: Through his preaching, the proud will be humbled and the humble lifted up—a reversal often seen in scripture.

f.w: many high ones shall be brought low

chapters.n: His voice is to rebuke sin and silence slander.

f.g: Stubborn wickedness; twisting of truth.

chapters.n: One of the most loved verses in the Doctrine and Covenants: humility brings the Lord’s guiding hand and answers to prayer.
The Lord knows Thomas loves his quorum, but he should not love them more than others; his love should reach everyone who loves the Lord’s name.

f.w: let thy love abound unto all men

f.g: Favoring some over others.

chapters.n: Thomas is to pray for the Twelve and correct them firmly. In 1837 several apostles were caught up in the dissent following the Kirtland bank’s failure.

f.g: Warn or correct earnestly.

chapters.n: After trials, the Lord will reach out to the apostles; if they stay soft-hearted, they will be converted and healed. Some of them later fell away; others returned.

f.g: An image of a stubborn ox resisting the yoke; to be stubborn or proud.

chapters.n: The message for Thomas applies to all the Twelve: get ready, take up the cross, follow Christ, and care for his flock—echoing Jesus’ charge to Peter.

f.w: take up your cross, follow me

chapters.n: A warning against pride and rebellion toward Joseph Smith, who holds keys that will remain with him until the Lord comes. Thomas Marsh himself left the Church the next year, returning in 1857.

f.w: rebel not against my servant Joseph
f.g: Several apostles, including Thomas B. Marsh in 1838, later turned against Joseph.

f.w: shall not be taken from him till I come

chapters.n: As President of the Twelve, Thomas held the keys of the kingdom for the Twelve’s work among the nations.
The Twelve were to open the work in places where the First Presidency—Joseph, Sidney, and Hyrum—could not personally go.

f.g: Hyrum Smith became a counselor in the First Presidency in November 1837, a few months after this revelation.

chapters.n: The First Presidency carried the burden of all the churches for the time being.

f.w: the burden of all the churches

chapters.n: Wherever the Presidency sends the Twelve, the Lord will be with them and open a door for the word to be received.

f.g: A real opportunity that leads to results.

chapters.n: Receiving Christ’s word means receiving him—and receiving the prophets he sends. The First Presidency are counselors to the Twelve.

f.w: Whosoever receiveth my word receiveth me

chapters.n: Missionaries sent by the Twelve, properly recommended and authorized, have power to open the kingdom to any nation.
Their power depends on humility, staying true to God’s word, and listening to the Spirit.

f.w: hearken to the voice of my Spirit

chapters.n: The Lord describes the spiritual condition of the world: darkness on the earth and deep darkness in people’s minds.

f.w: darkness covereth the earth, and gross darkness the minds of the people

f.g: Thick, dense.

chapters.n: Judgment is coming quickly—a day of burning, desolation, and mourning sweeping the earth like a whirlwind.
Sobering: judgment begins with the Lord’s own house—his Church—and then goes outward.

f.w: upon my house shall it begin

chapters.n: Especially those who claim to know the Lord but do not, and who blaspheme in the midst of his house. In 1837, apostasy in Kirtland was severe.
The Twelve are told not to get entangled in the troubled affairs of the Kirtland church, but to focus on their mission.

f.g: Kirtland, which was then torn by financial crisis and dissent.

chapters.n: First purify your hearts; then go preach to every creature who has not received the gospel.

f.w: preach my gospel unto every creature

chapters.n: Quoting Mark, the Lord restates the necessity of faith and baptism. “Damned” means stopped in progress, unable to receive the fullest blessings.

f.w: he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved

f.g: Condemned; in Latter-day Saint usage, halted in eternal progress.

chapters.n: The Twelve and First Presidency hold priesthood power for the last days—the dispensation of the fulness of times, when all past dispensations come together.

f.w: dispensation of the fulness of times

chapters.n: Their authority links them with every prophet who has held a dispensation since the creation.

f.w: from the beginning of the creation

chapters.n: These keys came down from the ancient fathers and were finally restored from heaven—by Peter, James, John, Moses, Elias, and Elijah.

f.w: being sent down from heaven unto you

chapters.n: The calling is great, so the Twelve must keep their hearts and lives clean, or they will be accountable for this generation.

f.w: Cleanse your hearts and your garments

chapters.n: Be faithful until the Lord returns; he will reward each person according to his works. Alpha and Omega—the first and last Greek letters—mean the Beginning and the End.
In March 1838 at Far West, Missouri, Joseph Smith recorded answers to questions about Isaiah 11. The first asks who the “Stem of Jesse” is. Jesse was the father of King David.

f.g: The trunk or stump of a tree; Isaiah pictures David’s fallen dynasty sprouting again.

chapters.n: The answer is simple and clear: the Stem is Jesus Christ, the royal descendant of David through whom the family line lives on.
Next question: what is the “rod” that comes from the stem? A rod here is a new shoot or branch.

f.g: A shoot or twig growing from a stump.

chapters.n: The rod is a servant in Christ’s hands, descended from both Jesse (Judah) and Ephraim (Joseph), with great power. The revelation does not name him; many Latter-day Saints believe it refers to Joseph Smith or to a latter-day prophetic leader.

f.w: a servant in the hands of Christ

chapters.n: Third question: who is the “root of Jesse” in Isaiah 11:10?

The root is a descendant of both Jesse and Joseph who holds the priesthood and its keys by right, to raise an “ensign” and gather God’s people in the last days. Again unnamed; many see Joseph Smith here.

f.g: A banner or flag raised as a rallying point.

f.w: the priesthood, and the keys of the kingdom

chapters.n: Elias Higbee, a Church leader in Far West, asks about Isaiah 52:1: “Put on thy strength, O Zion.” What does it mean, and whom did Isaiah mean?

f.w: Put on thy strength, O Zion

chapters.n: Isaiah meant those called in the last days to hold priesthood power to bring back Zion and redeem Israel. To “put on strength” is to take up priesthood authority—a birthright by lineage that Israel had lost and is invited to reclaim.

f.w: to put on her strength is to put on the authority of the priesthood

chapters.n: The next question is about Isaiah 52:2, where Zion is told to loose the bands from her neck.

f.w: loosing herself from the bands of her neck

chapters.n: Scattered Israel is urged to return to the Lord; if they do, he will speak to them again through revelation. The “bands” are the curses of a scattered, captive condition. Coming back to God breaks those chains.

f.g: Bonds or chains, like a captive’s collar.

chapters.n: David W. Patten, a senior member of the Twelve, is told to wrap up his business and sell his goods so he can go on a mission with the whole quorum the following spring. Sadly, he was killed in the Battle of Crooked River in October 1838, becoming an early apostle-martyr.

f.g: Ordained an apostle in 1835; he died October 25, 1838, after being wounded at Crooked River, Missouri.

f.w: make a disposition of his merchandise
f.g: Sell off or otherwise dispose of his stock of goods.

chapters.n: Some leaders were denying the Lord in 1838; their positions would be given to others. “Bishopric” here means office or calling in general, not a bishop’s office specifically.

f.w: others shall be planted in their stead

f.g: An office or position of responsibility (as in Acts 1:20, KJV).

chapters.n: This April 26, 1838, revelation at Far West is addressed first to the First Presidency—Joseph Smith, Sidney Rigdon, and Hyrum Smith—and their counselors.

f.w: your counselors who are and shall be appointed hereafter
f.g: Assistant counselors were also appointed to the First Presidency in this period.

chapters.n: It is also addressed to Edward Partridge, the bishop in Missouri, and his counselors.
And to the high council in Zion and all members worldwide. The Lord now gives his Church its formal name.

f.w: scattered abroad in all the world

chapters.n: The Church’s name is revealed: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. It puts Christ at the center and identifies members as “saints”—believers—in the last days.

f.w: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints

f.g: “Saint” in the New Testament means a member of the community of believers, not a perfect person. Earlier names included “Church of Christ” and “Church of the Latter Day Saints.”

chapters.n: Echoing Isaiah, the Saints are called to rise and let their light become a banner other nations can see and follow.

f.g: A flag or banner raised as a rallying point.

chapters.n: Gathering to Zion and its stakes offers protection and refuge from spiritual and physical storms in the last days.

f.g: Undiluted, in full strength.

chapters.n: Far West is declared holy ground—language recalling God’s words to Moses at the burning bush.

f.w: the ground upon which thou standest is holy

chapters.n: The Saints are commanded to build a temple in Far West as a gathering place for worship.
Preparatory work and a foundation are to begin that summer.

f.g: Cornerstones for the Far West Temple were laid July 4, 1838.

chapters.n: The work is to begin on July 4, 1838—a date chosen with patriotic significance—and continue diligently.

f.w: the fourth day of July next
f.g: The cornerstones were laid on Independence Day 1838, as commanded.

chapters.n: Exactly one year later they are to recommence laying the foundation. Though mobs drove the Saints out that winter, apostles secretly returned on April 26, 1839, to fulfill this command.

f.w: in one year from this day

chapters.n: Once begun, the work should continue until the temple is entirely finished, top to bottom.

f.g: The foundation stone at a building’s corner, laid first.

chapters.n: Debt had nearly crushed the Church after Kirtland. The Lord instructs the First Presidency not to go into debt again to build a temple.
The temple must follow a pattern the Lord himself will reveal—as with Moses’ tabernacle and the Kirtland Temple.
If the Saints don’t follow the revealed pattern, the Lord will not accept the building.
If they do follow it, as shown through Joseph and his counselors, the Lord will accept it from his people.
Far West should be built up quickly as Saints gather there.

f.g: Far West grew rapidly in 1838, reaching an estimated several thousand people before the Saints were expelled that winter.

chapters.n: Other nearby places would become stakes as Joseph received direction, such as Adam-ondi-Ahman.

f.w: other places should be appointed for stakes

chapters.n: The Lord stands behind Joseph and has given him the keys of the kingdom and ministry.

On May 19, 1838, a hill in Daviess County, Missouri, called Spring Hill, is named Adam-ondi-Ahman. The Lord reveals it as the place where Adam—the “Ancient of Days” in Daniel’s vision—will come to meet his posterity before the Second Coming. Latter-day Saints understand this as a great council where Adam reports to Christ.

f.g: Joseph Smith never fully defined the term; it is often understood to mean something like “the place or land of God where Adam dwelt.”

chapters.n: William Marks and Newel K. Whitney, leaders still in Kirtland, are told to settle their affairs and move to Missouri before winter. Many faithful Saints had already left the troubled Ohio community.

f.w: before I, the Lord, send again the snows
f.g: That is, before winter 1838–39.

chapters.n: Three urgent verbs—awake, arise, come forth—stress that they must not delay.

f.g: Delay, linger.

chapters.n: Delay would bring them harm. Kirtland was no longer the gathering place.

f.w: it shall not be well with them

chapters.n: The Lord asks a famous question: “What is property unto me?” He created everything; clinging to possessions is a spiritual danger.

f.g: Strong desire for possessions, especially what belongs to others.

chapters.n: Let Kirtland property go to pay debts. Whatever remains, they may keep. Don’t let land hold you back from following God.

f.g: Sold or handed over to satisfy creditors.

chapters.n: God owns the birds, fish, beasts, and the earth itself, and he controls the fate of nations. He doesn’t need anyone’s land.

f.w: Have I not made the earth?

chapters.n: God can make empty, lonely places bloom and produce abundantly—so trust him for a new beginning.

f.w: make solitary places to bud and to blossom

chapters.n: There is plenty of room in Missouri, at Adam-ondi-Ahman and the plains of Olaha Shinehah, where Adam lived. Why covet a “drop” in Kirtland and miss weightier things?

f.g: A name for the plains near Adam-ondi-Ahman; “Shinehah” appears elsewhere as a name for the sun.

chapters.n: So come to Zion, the land of God’s people.

f.g: Here, the Saints’ gathering area in northern Missouri.

chapters.n: William Marks, if faithful in small things, will be given greater responsibility. He is to preside at Far West. He later served as stake president in Nauvoo.

Newel K. Whitney is rebuked for being caught up with a worldly group and for “littleness of soul.” He is to come to Adam-ondi-Ahman and be a bishop in deed, not just in name. He accepted the correction and served faithfully.

f.g: In Revelation, the Nicolaitans were a group in the early church condemned for compromising with worldliness; here, apostates and money-minded men in Kirtland.
Narrowness or pettiness of spirit.

chapters.n: Oliver Granger, a less prominent member, is singled out for praise: his name will be honored forever. The Lord sees faithfulness that the world overlooks.
Oliver Granger was assigned to settle the First Presidency’s debts in Kirtland. The Lord says even if he “falls” (fails), he will rise; his sacrifice matters more to God than his success.

f.w: his sacrifice shall be more sacred unto me than his increase
f.g: A key principle: God values faithful effort over measurable results.

chapters.n: He too should come to Zion, where he will act as a merchant for the Saints’ benefit.

f.g: An agent handling business on behalf of the Church.

chapters.n: No one should look down on Oliver Granger; the Saints should bless him forever.

f.g: Look down on, scorn.

chapters.n: The Saints remaining in Kirtland must keep the temple holy. The Lord will in his time “overthrow the moneychangers”—as Jesus cleansed the temple of those turning worship into profit.
By July 1838 several apostles had left the Church. The Lord directs that a conference be held immediately to reorganize the Twelve and fill the vacancies.

f.g: Apostles such as William E. McLellin, Luke and Lyman Johnson, and John F. Boynton had been excommunicated or had left.

chapters.n: Thomas B. Marsh, the quorum president, is to remain in Missouri for a while to publish the Lord’s word.

f.g: Thomas Marsh was involved with the Church’s periodical, the Elders’ Journal.

chapters.n: The rest are to begin preaching immediately. If they serve with humility, meekness, and patience, the Lord will provide for their families and open doors for their work.

f.g: Patience under trial or provocation.

chapters.n: Next spring they are to cross “the great waters”—the Atlantic—to preach the fulness of the gospel in Great Britain.

f.g: Proclaim publicly; make widely known.

chapters.n: They must formally depart from the Far West temple site on April 26, 1839. Though the Saints had been driven from Missouri, several apostles returned secretly at night on that date and fulfilled the command.

f.w: the twenty-sixth day of April next

chapters.n: Four new apostles are named: John Taylor, John E. Page, Wilford Woodruff, and Willard Richards. Taylor and Woodruff would later become Presidents of the Church.

f.g: Fourth President of the Church (1889–1898); he issued the Manifesto (Official Declaration 1).

chapters.n: Joseph had prayed, “O Lord, show unto thy servants how much thou requirest of the properties of thy people for a tithing.” The answer begins: members should first give their surplus property to the bishop in Zion.

f.g: What a family had beyond its reasonable needs.

f.w: the bishop of my church in Zion

chapters.n: These funds were to build the temple, lay Zion’s foundation, support priesthood work, and pay the First Presidency’s debts.
This initial offering marks the beginning of tithing as a formal law in the restored Church.

f.g: From Old English for “a tenth.”

chapters.n: After that first gift, members are to pay one-tenth of their “interest” each year. Church leaders have explained “interest” as income. This is a permanent law for supporting the Lord’s work.

f.w: one-tenth of all their interest annually
f.g: Interest = increase or income.
A permanent, ongoing law.

chapters.n: Everyone gathering to Zion must keep this law to be considered worthy to live among the Saints.

f.w: shall be tithed of their surplus properties

chapters.n: Tithing is part of how Zion becomes holy. If the Saints don’t keep it, the land will not be Zion for them—it’s the people’s hearts, not the location, that make Zion.
This law serves as an “ensample”—an example or model—for every stake.

f.g: An older form of “example.”

chapters.n: The same day tithing was revealed, the Lord set up a council to decide how tithes are used: the First Presidency, the Presiding Bishop’s office, and a high council—guided by the Lord’s own voice. Today the Council on the Disposition of the Tithes (First Presidency, Quorum of the Twelve, and Presiding Bishopric) continues this pattern.

f.g: Disposed of = allotted, directed, spent.

f.w: by mine own voice unto them

chapters.n: Joseph Smith had been imprisoned for months in the cold, cramped lower room of Liberty Jail while the Saints were driven from Missouri. In a letter dated March 20, 1839, he cries out like the psalmists: where is God? Why is he hidden?

f.g: A tent or canopy; here, the covering that seems to hide God from view.

chapters.n: How long will God hold back while he sees and hears his people’s suffering? Joseph’s honesty with God models real prayer in anguish.

f.g: Held back, restrained.

chapters.n: Joseph asks how long the injustices will go on before God’s heart is moved. “Bowels” in old English meant the inner seat of tender feelings.

f.g: Bowels = innermost feelings; compassion felt deep inside.

chapters.n: Joseph reminds God—and himself—that God created everything and controls even the devil and hell. Then comes a rush of pleas: reach out, see, hear, uncover, soften.

f.g: Hebrew for the realm of the dead; the underworld.
Overtaken by darkness.

chapters.n: Joseph asks God to defend his people against their enemies—an honest, raw cry for justice, like the imprecatory psalms.
He closes his plea simply: remember your suffering Saints, and we will praise you forever.
The Lord answers tenderly, calling Joseph “my son.” Compared to eternity, his trials will be brief. These words have comforted countless people in hard times.

f.w: My son, peace be unto thy soul

chapters.n: The key is not just enduring, but enduring well—with faith and without bitterness. Then God will lift him up.
Joseph is reminded that many friends still stand by him and will welcome him warmly again.

f.w: Thy friends do stand by thee
f.g: Saints such as Emma Smith, Brigham Young, and others continued to support him and visited or wrote to him in jail.

chapters.n: Joseph is not as badly off as Job, whose friends accused him of secret sin. Perspective can ease suffering.

f.w: Thou art not yet as Job

chapters.n: Those falsely accusing Joseph will see their hopes vanish like frost melting under the morning sun.

f.g: White frost formed on cold mornings.

chapters.n: God has determined to change circumstances and will let schemers be caught in their own cleverness.

f.w: take them in their own craftiness

f.g: Formally decreed, as with a signature and wax seal.

chapters.n: What they wish on others will come back on themselves—a common biblical principle of justice.
Their plans against the Saints will be disappointed.

f.w: their hopes may be cut off

chapters.n: A strong prophetic warning that persecutors and their families would not endure. “To stand by the wall” is a biblical idiom for surviving descendants.

f.w: not one of them is left to stand by the wall
f.g: An idiom from Old Testament curses meaning no one survives.

chapters.n: Cursed are those who “lift up the heel”—turn against—the Lord’s anointed, accusing them of sin when they have done what God commanded.

f.g: To kick or turn against, especially in betrayal.
Right, proper.

chapters.n: Those who loudly accuse God’s servants of sin often act from their own sin and rebellion.
Some had sworn false testimony to put Church leaders in prison or get them killed. Several former members testified against Joseph in Missouri.
They have harmed the Lord’s “little ones”—his humble followers—and will be cut off from temple blessings.
Their prosperity will fail, and even those who once flattered them will despise them.

f.w: Their basket shall not be full

chapters.n: They forfeit the right to the priesthood for themselves and their descendants who follow them in that course.

f.w: They shall not have right to the priesthood
f.g: Priesthood is held by righteousness; persistent opposition to God’s work forfeits it.

chapters.n: Echoing Jesus’ words, it would be better for them to drown with a millstone around their necks.

f.w: a millstone had been hanged about their necks

f.g: A heavy round stone for grinding grain.

chapters.n: Woe to those who trouble, drive, murder, and testify against God’s people. Jesus called the hypocrites of his day “a generation of vipers.”

f.g: Distress, trouble.

chapters.n: God sees all their deeds and has a swift judgment held in reserve at the right time.

f.g: At its proper, appointed time.

chapters.n: Every person has an appointed time to answer for their works.

f.w: a time appointed for every man

chapters.n: The tone turns hopeful. God will reveal knowledge by the Holy Ghost that has never been revealed before—a promise Joseph saw fulfilled in Nauvoo.

f.w: the unspeakable gift of the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Ancient prophets looked forward eagerly to this day; angels pointed them to it as reserved for the completion of their glory.
In this coming time nothing will be withheld—including truths about God and other divine beings.

f.w: whether there be one God or many gods

chapters.n: Heavenly thrones and powers will be revealed to—and bestowed on—those who stay valiant in the gospel of Jesus Christ.

f.w: thrones and dominions, principalities and powers

chapters.n: Even the limits of the heavens, seas, land, sun, moon, and stars will be revealed.

f.g: The boundaries, laws, and limits of the universe.

chapters.n: All the cycles, times, laws, and glories of the heavenly bodies will be revealed in the dispensation of the fulness of times.

f.g: Orbits or rotations of heavenly bodies.

f.w: dispensation of the fulness of times

chapters.n: This was planned in a council of the eternal God before the world was created—to be revealed at the end, when everyone enters God’s presence and rest.
Joseph gives a vivid image: trying to stop God from pouring knowledge on the Saints is like trying to stop the Missouri River with your arm. Running water cleans itself; truth will prevail.

f.w: How long can rolling waters remain impure?
f.g: Moving water purifies itself over time—an image of truth overcoming error.
Small and weak.

chapters.n: A famous question: many are called to serve, but few are chosen. Why?

f.w: many called, but few are chosen

chapters.n: Because their hearts are set on worldly things and on people’s praise, they miss the essential lesson that follows.

f.w: aspire to the honors of men

chapters.n: The lesson: priesthood rights are bound to heaven’s powers, and those powers work only through righteousness. Authority without goodness is empty.

f.g: The actual power of God that makes priesthood effective, distinct from the office itself.

chapters.n: Priesthood can be conferred, but when someone uses it to hide sin, feed pride, or control others unrighteously “in any degree,” heaven withdraws. “Amen to the priesthood” means it is finished for that man.

f.g: That is, the end of it; his priesthood power ceases.
Force or pressure that overrides another’s will.

chapters.n: Before he knows it, such a person is left alone, fighting God like an ox kicking against the goad.

f.g: Pricks = sharp goads used to drive oxen; kicking them only hurts the ox.
Before.

chapters.n: A frank warning learned through hard experience: almost everyone who gets a little authority is tempted to misuse it.

f.g: Using position or power to control, manipulate, or force others.

chapters.n: That is why many are called but few are chosen.

f.g: For this reason.

chapters.n: True influence comes not from position but from persuasion, patience, gentleness, meekness, and sincere love. This applies to parents, leaders, and spouses as much as priesthood holders.

f.g: Genuine, sincere love; not faked.
Convincing by reason and love rather than force.

chapters.n: Add kindness and true knowledge, which expand the soul—without hypocrisy or deceit.

f.g: Without deceit or trickery.
