chapters.n: Sometimes correction is needed—“betimes” means promptly or at the right time, and only when prompted by the Holy Ghost. Afterward, show more love so the person knows you are not an enemy.

f.g: Early, promptly; at the appropriate moment (not “sometimes”).
Clarity and directness, not harshness or anger.

chapters.n: So he will know your loyalty is stronger than death itself.
Be full of charity toward everyone and let virtue adorn your thoughts constantly. Then confidence before God grows, and priesthood understanding settles on the soul gently, like dew.

f.w: let virtue garnish thy thoughts unceasingly
f.g: Garnish = decorate, adorn.

f.w: distil upon thy soul as the dews from heaven

chapters.n: The promised result: the Holy Ghost as a constant companion, a scepter of righteousness, and an everlasting dominion that comes freely, without force—because it rests on love.

f.g: A ruler’s staff, symbol of authority.

chapters.n: Still in Liberty Jail, Joseph receives a striking promise: people across the world will ask about his name. Some will mock him, and hell will rage against him. This echoes what Moroni told the teenage Joseph in 1823.

f.w: The ends of the earth shall inquire after thy name

f.g: Mockery, ridicule.

chapters.n: Meanwhile the pure, wise, noble, and virtuous will constantly seek his counsel and blessings.

f.g: Through his direction and the blessings he gives by laying on hands.

chapters.n: Traitors’ testimony will never turn the Lord’s people against Joseph as a whole.

f.g: Some former associates had testified against Joseph in Missouri courts.

chapters.n: Though their influence has put him behind bars, he will be honored. His voice will be more powerful than a lion among his enemies because of his righteousness, and God will stand by him forever.

f.g: Liberty Jail had stone walls about four feet thick and barred windows.

f.w: more terrible in the midst of thine enemies than the fierce lion
f.g: Terrible = awe-inspiring, commanding.

chapters.n: The Lord lists hardships Joseph may face, echoing Paul’s list of perils.

A painfully personal list: false accusations, separation from family, and being torn at swordpoint from his wife and children—while his six-year-old son Joseph III clings to him crying, “My father, why can’t you stay with us?” This had actually happened at his arrest in Far West.

f.w: thine elder son, although but six years of age
f.g: Joseph Smith III, born November 1832, was nearly six at Joseph’s arrest in November 1838.

f.w: like wolves for the blood of the lamb

chapters.n: Even if every danger comes—death sentence, storms, shipwreck, blackened skies, the jaws of hell—Joseph is told that all of it will give him experience and be for his good. Suffering can shape and teach.

f.w: all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good
the sentence of death passed upon thee
f.g: In November 1838 a militia court-martial ordered Joseph shot; General Alexander Doniphan refused to carry it out.

chapters.n: The heart of the revelation: Jesus Christ descended below all suffering. No one has suffered more than he. “Art thou greater than he?”

f.w: The Son of Man hath descended below them all

chapters.n: So keep going. Enemies have limits they cannot pass. Joseph’s lifespan is known to God and will not be cut short—so he need not fear what people can do.

f.w: their bounds are set, they cannot pass
fear not what man can do

chapters.n: Continuing his Liberty Jail letter, Joseph suggests the Saints document everything they have suffered at the hands of Missourians. Careful records would support appeals for justice.

f.g: Fitness, appropriateness.

chapters.n: They should record property losses and damages—to reputation, body, and land.

f.g: Land and buildings, as opposed to movable goods.

chapters.n: They should also record the names of those involved in the oppression, as far as possible.

f.g: Unjust and cruel treatment.

chapters.n: A committee might gather sworn statements and collect libelous publications. Hundreds of Saints later wrote such petitions, which were sent to Congress.

f.g: Written statements sworn under oath.
Falsely damaging to someone’s reputation in print.

chapters.n: They should gather negative reports from magazines, encyclopedias, and histories and present the full chain of wickedness done against the Saints.

f.g: A linked chain or series.
Wicked, villainous.

chapters.n: These records should be published worldwide and presented to government leaders—a last required effort before the Saints could fully claim God’s promise to intervene, so the nation would be left without excuse.

f.w: present them to the heads of government

chapters.n: This is a solemn duty to God, angels, and families crushed by grief. Joseph traces the persecution to a spirit that has fastened inherited false creeds onto people’s hearts and filled the world with confusion.

f.w: the creeds of the fathers, who have inherited lies

f.g: The main driving spring of a clock; the chief cause.

chapters.n: Joseph piles up images of captivity—yoke, bands, handcuffs, chains, fetters—to show how such a spirit binds people.

f.g: Chains for the feet.

chapters.n: The duty extends to widows and orphans whose husbands and fathers were killed—such as at the Hawn’s Mill massacre in October 1838.

f.g: About 17 Latter-day Saint men and boys were killed at Hawn’s Mill on October 30, 1838.

chapters.n: Such deeds are so dark they would make hell shudder and the devil’s hands tremble.

f.g: To shake or become paralyzed.

chapters.n: It is also a duty owed to the rising generation and to all the pure in heart.

f.g: Young people and future generations.

chapters.n: Many good people in every church are blinded by others’ cunning and kept from truth only because they don’t know where to find it—a hopeful and generous view of other faiths.

f.w: only kept from the truth because they know not where to find it

chapters.n: So the Saints should spend their lives bringing hidden evils to light, as revealed from heaven.

f.w: bringing to light all the hidden things of darkness

chapters.n: These duties should be done with real earnestness.

f.g: Serious, sincere effort.

chapters.n: Don’t treat these as small matters; much in the Saints’ future depends on them.

f.g: The future.

chapters.n: A memorable image: a small helm (rudder) steers a huge ship in a storm, keeping it “workways”—positioned to ride the wind and waves. Small acts can change great outcomes.

f.g: In a workable position; headed so the ship can handle the storm.

chapters.n: Do everything in our power cheerfully, and then stand still with full confidence to see God’s salvation—as Moses told Israel at the Red Sea.

f.w: let us cheerfully do all things that lie in our power
f.g: A widely quoted principle: do your part, then trust God.

f.w: stand still, with the utmost assurance, to see the salvation of God

chapters.n: By January 19, 1841, the Saints had found refuge at Nauvoo, Illinois, after being expelled from Missouri. The Lord accepts Joseph’s offering and explains he raised Joseph up to show divine wisdom through humble, “weak” people.

f.w: the weak things of the earth

chapters.n: Joseph is to issue a formal proclamation of the gospel and of Nauvoo as a stake—a “cornerstone of Zion”—to be refined and beautiful like a palace.

f.g: Nauvoo was to be a central, foundational stake for the gathering.

f.w: after the similitude of a palace

chapters.n: The proclamation is to go to world rulers, the U.S. president-elect (William Henry Harrison), state governors, and all nations.

f.g: William Henry Harrison had been elected in November 1840 and took office in March 1841.

chapters.n: It should be written with meekness and under the Holy Ghost’s influence.
The Spirit will show Joseph what lies ahead for these rulers.

f.g: Befall = happen to.

chapters.n: The Lord will call on rulers to pay attention to Zion, because the appointed time to favor her has come.

f.w: the set time has come to favor her

chapters.n: Speak boldly and without fear; earthly rulers are like grass and fading flowers. The warning leaves them without excuse.
If they reject the Lord’s servants, at his coming they will be counted with the hypocrites in sorrow and regret.

f.w: unveil the face of my covering

chapters.n: Yet the Lord will soften many rulers’ hearts, so the Saints will find favor and the Gentiles will help lift up Zion.

f.g: Grace here = favor.

chapters.n: The Lord’s coming will be sudden; where will his people find safety? The question urges preparation.

f.w: in an hour when ye think not

chapters.n: Echoing Isaiah, kings are invited to bring their wealth to help God’s people and build up Zion.

f.w: with your gold and your silver

chapters.n: Robert B. Thompson, Joseph’s clerk, is to help write the proclamation. He died later that year at age 30.

f.g: Church clerk and editor of the Times and Seasons; he died in August 1841.

chapters.n: If he follows Joseph’s counsel and stays faithful, he will be richly blessed and great in God’s eyes.

f.g: A great number; abundance.

chapters.n: But the Lord will hold him accountable for his stewardship.

f.g: A responsibility entrusted by God, for which one must give an account.

chapters.n: Hyrum Smith is praised: the Lord loves him for his integrity and love of right. Hyrum was known for unwavering loyalty.
John C. Bennett, a recent convert who was then mayor-elect of Nauvoo, is to help—with blessings conditional on accepting counsel.

f.g: Bennett later fell into serious immorality, was excommunicated in 1842, and became a bitter opponent; the condition here proved significant.

chapters.n: The Lord accepts Bennett’s work “if he continue.” Promises in scripture are often conditional on faithfulness.

f.w: which I accept if he continue

chapters.n: Lyman Wight is to keep preaching for Zion humbly; the Lord will carry him “as on eagles’ wings.”
When Lyman finishes, the Lord will receive him as he has received David Patten, Edward Partridge, and Joseph Smith Sr.—who sits with Abraham. A glimpse into the faithful dead.

f.g: The Prophet’s father, first Patriarch of the Church, died September 1840.

chapters.n: George Miller is praised as honest and trustworthy, with a love for the Lord’s testimony.
George Miller is called as a bishop to receive consecrated offerings and bless the poor.

f.g: Offerings dedicated to the Lord’s work.

chapters.n: George Miller, Lyman Wight, John Snider, and others are to build a boarding house on a site Joseph will show them.

f.w: build a house unto my name

chapters.n: It is to be a fine inn where travelers can rest, find health and safety, and ponder the Lord’s word.
The house must be kept clean and holy under its appointed manager, or the Lord will not dwell there.

f.w: the governor which shall be appointed
f.g: Governor = manager or overseer.

chapters.n: All Saints from far away are to gather.

f.w: let all my saints come from afar

chapters.n: Messengers should invite people to bring precious materials and antiquities to build the temple—recalling how Israel brought fine materials for the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple.

f.w: the box tree, and the fir tree, and the pine tree

f.g: Ancient objects or relics.

chapters.n: Iron, copper, brass, zinc, and precious things will help build a house for the Most High.

f.w: build a house to my name

chapters.n: There is no place on earth where the Lord can restore the “fulness of the priesthood.” Higher ordinances require a temple.

f.g: The highest priesthood blessings, received through temple ordinances such as the endowment and sealing.

chapters.n: There is no baptismal font for baptisms for the dead—an ordinance Joseph had introduced in August 1840.

f.w: baptized for those who are dead

chapters.n: This ordinance belongs in the temple and is acceptable elsewhere only while the Saints are too poor to build one. Early proxy baptisms were done in the Mississippi River.

f.w: only in the days of your poverty
f.g: Before the Nauvoo Temple font was dedicated in November 1841, these baptisms were done in rivers.

chapters.n: The Lord gives a grace period: while they build, baptisms outside the temple are acceptable.

f.g: An appointed period of grace.

chapters.n: After that time, such baptisms won’t be accepted, and if the Saints fail to build, they will be rejected as a church with their dead. The temple was essential.

f.w: rejected as a church, with your dead

chapters.n: Baptism for the dead was instituted before the world was created and belongs in God’s house.

f.w: from before the foundation of the world

chapters.n: The temple holds the keys of the priesthood that bring honor and glory.
After this time, baptisms for the dead done by scattered members outside the temple won’t be accepted.

f.g: Members living away from the central gathering place.

chapters.n: Such baptisms belong in Zion, its stakes, and Jerusalem—the appointed places of refuge where temples would be.

f.w: in Zion, and in her stakes, and in Jerusalem

chapters.n: How can washings be acceptable except in a house built to the Lord’s name? Ordinances need sacred space.

f.g: Ritual cleansing ordinances; compare the Mosaic washings of priests.

chapters.n: This is why Moses built a portable tabernacle and Israel later a temple: to reveal ordinances hidden since before the world.

f.w: I commanded Moses that he should build a tabernacle

chapters.n: A long list of temple ordinances and functions—anointings, washings, baptisms for the dead, solemn assemblies, offerings by the sons of Levi, and holy-place revelations—all belong to the Lord’s house.

f.w: memorials for your sacrifices by the sons of Levi

f.g: Revelations or divine communications.
Probably citizens or communities of Zion.

chapters.n: Build this house so the Lord may reveal his ordinances in it.
The Lord will reveal things hidden since before creation, belonging to this final dispensation.

f.g: Condescend graciously; be willing.

f.w: kept hid from before the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Joseph will be shown everything about the temple—its priesthood and its site.

f.w: I will show unto my servant Joseph all things

chapters.n: The site they had already considered—on the bluff overlooking the Mississippi—is the Lord’s choice.

f.w: the spot which I have chosen
f.g: The Nauvoo Temple was built on a bluff above the city; it was rebuilt on the same site and dedicated in 2002.

chapters.n: If they work with all their might, the Lord will make the spot holy.

f.g: Make sacred; set apart for holy use.

chapters.n: If the Saints follow the Lord and his appointed leaders, they will not be moved from their place.

f.w: they shall not be moved out of their place

chapters.n: If they don’t listen, they won’t be blessed, because they defile holy ground and ordinances. The Saints were in fact driven from Nauvoo in 1846.

f.g: Formal grants or founding documents; here, sacred authorizations.

chapters.n: A clear warning: building a temple without obedience won’t bring the promised blessings.

f.w: I will not perform the oath

chapters.n: Disobedience turns blessings into curses—by their own choices.

f.g: Foolish acts.

chapters.n: A comforting principle: when people try with all their might to do God’s work but enemies stop them, God accepts their offering and no longer requires the work of them.

f.g: It is fitting or proper for me.

chapters.n: The guilt falls on those who obstructed God’s work, as long as they refuse to repent.

f.w: unto the third and fourth generation

chapters.n: This is why the Lord accepted the efforts of those commanded to build Zion and a temple in Jackson County who were prevented by enemies.
Judgment rests on those who drove them out and refuse to repent.
This is given as comfort for all who have been hindered by enemies from doing God’s work.

f.g: Consolation = comfort in loss or disappointment.

chapters.n: The Lord will save all the pure-hearted Saints killed in Missouri.

f.w: slain in the land of Missouri

chapters.n: Again the command: build a temple here in Nauvoo, to prove faithfulness and receive honor, immortality, and eternal life.
The boarding house is to bear the Lord’s name, and Joseph’s family should have a place in it permanently.

f.w: let my name be named upon it
f.g: Dedicated to the Lord’s purposes.

chapters.n: Joseph’s anointing and blessing extend to his descendants.
The Lord repeats to Joseph the Abrahamic promise: through you and your seed all the families of the earth will be blessed.

f.w: In thee and in thy seed shall the kindred of the earth be blessed

chapters.n: So Joseph’s family will have a place in that house forever.

f.g: Emma Smith and her family did live in the partly finished Nauvoo House after Joseph’s death.

chapters.n: It shall be called the Nauvoo House—a pleasant inn where travelers can rest and admire Zion and the temple.

f.g: Never completed as planned; a portion was later finished as a home and still stands in Nauvoo.

chapters.n: Travelers may also receive counsel from leaders who are like noted plants and watchmen on the walls.
George Miller, Lyman Wight, John Snider, and Peter Haws are to organize as a quorum with a president to build the Nauvoo House.

f.g: The Nauvoo House Association was chartered by the Illinois legislature in 1841.

chapters.n: They should draft a constitution to sell shares of stock to finance the building.

f.g: Shares of ownership sold to raise money.

chapters.n: Shares must cost at least $50, and no one person may hold more than $15,000—preventing any single investor from controlling it.

f.g: A substantial sum in 1841, roughly a month or two of a laborer’s wages.

chapters.n: The maximum is repeated for emphasis: no more than $15,000 from one man.

f.g: Firm limits to protect fairness.

chapters.n: The minimum is repeated as well.

f.g: The minimum share price.

chapters.n: Stock is given only on actual payment—no credit or promises.

f.w: at the time he receives stock
f.g: Payment up front was required, likely to avoid the debt problems of Kirtland.

chapters.n: Shares are proportional to payment; no payment, no stock.

f.g: Equal to the amount paid in.

chapters.n: Stock belongs to the buyer and his heirs as long as they choose to keep it.

f.g: Transfer ownership legally.

chapters.n: The managers must use the money only for the Nauvoo House.

f.g: Take or use for a particular purpose.

chapters.n: Misusing funds without consent requires fourfold repayment, or the managers will be cursed and removed. God cannot be mocked.
Joseph himself is bound by the same limits—no special exemption for the Prophet.

f.g: The rules apply equally to all.

chapters.n: Others had asked what the Lord wanted of them; he now answers them individually.

f.w: they have asked it at my hands

chapters.n: Vinson Knight, a bishop, may invest in the house for his family.

f.g: A bishop in Nauvoo; he died in 1842.

chapters.n: Vinson should speak loudly for the poor and needy; his offerings will be accepted, unlike Cain’s.
His family should take heart; the Lord has chosen him and will forgive his sins.

f.w: I will forgive all his sins

chapters.n: Hyrum may invest as he sees fit.

f.g: As he thinks best.

chapters.n: Isaac Galland, who sold land to the Saints in Iowa and Illinois, may invest; the Lord loves him for his help and forgives his sins.

f.g: A land agent who helped the Saints acquire land near Commerce (Nauvoo) and joined the Church in 1839.

chapters.n: Galland is to be ordained by William Marks and travel with Hyrum on business Joseph assigns.

f.w: ordained by my servant William Marks
f.g: Marks was Nauvoo stake president.

chapters.n: William Marks may invest.
Henry G. Sherwood, a high councilor, may invest.
William Law, soon to be a counselor in the First Presidency, may invest.

f.g: He later turned against Joseph and helped publish the Nauvoo Expositor in 1844.

chapters.n: Law should not take his family back east to Kirtland. The Lord will one day build up Kirtland but has a scourge prepared for its current inhabitants.

f.g: A whip; a source of severe punishment or affliction.

chapters.n: Almon Babbitt, presiding in Kirtland, is rebuked for setting up his own counsel against the First Presidency and leading people to worship a “golden calf”—a false priority.

f.g: Seeks ambitiously.

chapters.n: No one who came to Nauvoo to keep God’s commandments should leave.

f.g: Trying, attempting.

chapters.n: Whether they live or die, let them do so in the Lord. The faithful dead rest from labor yet continue their work.

f.w: if they die let them die unto me

chapters.n: William Law worried about malaria and illness in swampy Nauvoo. The Lord says: trust me; keep the commandments, and even sickness will turn to your glory.

f.g: Malaria and other fevers were common in Nauvoo’s marshy riverfront.

f.w: If ye love me, keep my commandments

f.g: Contribute or result.

chapters.n: Law is to preach joyfully in nearby towns—Warsaw, Carthage, Burlington, and Madison—then await further instruction at conference.

f.g: Warsaw and Carthage were Illinois towns later hostile to the Saints; Joseph was killed at Carthage in 1844.

chapters.n: He should follow Joseph’s counsel, help the poor, and help publish Joseph’s new Bible translation.

f.w: the new translation of my holy word
f.g: Joseph Smith’s inspired revision of the Bible (JST); it was not fully published during his lifetime.

chapters.n: If he does, he will be blessed and his children will never beg for bread.

f.w: his seed be found begging bread

chapters.n: William Law is to replace Hyrum as counselor in the First Presidency so Hyrum can become Patriarch—an office his father held and blessed him to inherit.

f.g: Presiding Patriarch to the Church, who gives patriarchal blessings.

f.w: by blessing and also by right
f.g: Joseph Smith Sr., the first Patriarch, blessed Hyrum as his successor before dying in 1840.

chapters.n: Hyrum will hold the keys of patriarchal blessings for all the Church.
Those Hyrum blesses will be blessed; what he binds on earth will be bound in heaven—sealing power.

f.w: whatsoever he shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven

chapters.n: Hyrum is also made a prophet, seer, and revelator to the Church alongside Joseph.

f.w: a prophet, and a seer, and a revelator

chapters.n: Hyrum is to work together with Joseph and receive the blessings and priesthood once held by Oliver Cowdery—the “Second Elder” and Associate President, who had left the Church in 1838.

f.g: Oliver had been Associate President and second witness with Joseph of key restorations; he returned to the Church in 1848.

chapters.n: Hyrum will testify of what the Lord shows him, and his name will be honored forever. He died beside Joseph as a fellow witness.
William Law should also receive keys to ask and receive. If humble and without guile, the Comforter will teach him all truth and give him words in the moment.

f.w: in the very hour, what he shall say

chapters.n: Signs will follow him: healing, casting out devils, and protection from poison—as Jesus promised believers.
He will be protected from serpents and soar in his thoughts like an eagle.
If the Lord wills him to raise the dead, he should not hold back his voice.
Law should preach boldly with joy and hosannas to God on his throne.
The Lord has a special mission for William and Hyrum; Joseph is needed at home.

f.g: Stay home.

chapters.n: Sidney Rigdon, often sick and discouraged after Missouri, is invited to rise up, fulfill his calling as Joseph’s counselor, and humble himself.

f.w: if my servant Sidney will serve me
f.g: Sidney had suffered greatly in Missouri and was in poor health.

chapters.n: If Sidney offers an acceptable offering and stays with the Saints, he will be healed and again be a spokesman.
He should move his family near Joseph.

f.g: Settle his household.

chapters.n: In his travels he should warn the world like a trumpet to flee the coming wrath.
Sidney and William Law should help Joseph write the proclamation to the kings.

f.w: a solemn proclamation unto the kings of the earth

chapters.n: Sidney should not move east but relocate as directed.

f.g: Pennsylvania, Ohio, and the eastern states.

chapters.n: He should not look for safety outside Nauvoo. After Joseph’s death Sidney did leave for Pittsburgh.

f.g: Nauvoo is often said to mean “beautiful” or “beautiful place” in Hebrew.

chapters.n: Even now, if Sidney listens, all will be well with him.

f.w: it shall be well with him

chapters.n: Amos Davies is told to invest in the Nauvoo House.

f.g: A Nauvoo storekeeper and postmaster.

chapters.n: If he wants a share, he must follow Joseph’s counsel and work with his own hands to earn people’s trust.
Faithful in a few things, he will rule over many.
So he should humble himself to be exalted.

f.w: abase himself that he may be exalted

chapters.n: Robert D. Foster, a doctor and builder, is to build a house for Joseph as contracted.

f.g: Later a leading opponent of Joseph and co-publisher of the Nauvoo Expositor.

chapters.n: He must repent of folly, be charitable, stop doing evil, and stop harsh speech.
He should also invest in the Nauvoo House.

f.w: the quorum of the Nauvoo House
f.g: The board managing the building.

chapters.n: If he follows the counsel of Joseph, Hyrum, William Law, and other leaders, all will be well with him forever.
Only believers in the Book of Mormon and the revelations may invest in the Nauvoo House.

f.w: a believer in the Book of Mormon
f.g: Keeping the project in the hands of committed members.

chapters.n: Anything more or less than this comes from evil and brings curses.

f.w: more or less than this cometh of evil

chapters.n: The Nauvoo House committee should be fairly paid, at wages they agree on.

f.g: Fair payment.

chapters.n: Stockholders share the cost of wages if needed; otherwise the workers’ labor counts as stock.

f.g: Pay his fair share.

chapters.n: Now the Lord lists the officers of the Melchizedek Priesthood—named after the Son’s holy order—for Nauvoo.

f.w: after the order of mine Only Begotten Son

chapters.n: First, Hyrum Smith as Patriarch, holding sealing blessings by the Holy Spirit of Promise, which seals the faithful up to redemption.
Joseph is presiding elder over the whole Church—translator, revelator, seer, and prophet.

f.w: a translator, a revelator, a seer, and prophet

chapters.n: Sidney Rigdon and William Law are Joseph’s counselors; together they form the First Presidency.
Brigham Young is President of the Quorum of the Twelve—a calling that made him the senior leader after Joseph’s death.
The Twelve hold keys to open the kingdom everywhere and send the word to every creature.

f.w: the four corners of the earth

chapters.n: The other apostles are named. Several, like John Taylor and Wilford Woodruff, later became Church Presidents.

f.g: Joseph’s younger brother; he was later excommunicated (1845).

chapters.n: David Patten, killed in 1838, keeps his priesthood in the next life, but another may fill his calling. Priesthood continues beyond death.

f.w: his priesthood no man taketh from him

chapters.n: A high council is given to Nauvoo, the cornerstone stake.
The high councilors are named. Seymour Brunson had died; Aaron Johnson is to replace him.

f.w: Seymour Brunson I have taken unto myself
f.g: Brunson died in August 1840; Joseph first taught baptism for the dead publicly at his funeral.

chapters.n: Don Carlos Smith, Joseph’s youngest brother, is to preside over a quorum of high priests.

f.g: Don Carlos Smith died in August 1841 at age 25.

chapters.n: The high priests’ quorum prepares men to serve as stake presidents and other standing (local) officers.

f.g: Resident, local leaders, as opposed to traveling ministers.

chapters.n: They may travel, but their main calling is to preside locally.
Amasa Lyman and Noah Packard are his counselors.

f.g: Later an apostle.

chapters.n: John A. Hicks, Samuel Williams, and Jesse Baker preside over the elders, who are mainly local ministers.

f.g: Local, resident ministers.

chapters.n: Seven presidents are named over the seventies. Joseph Young was Brigham Young’s older brother.
The seventies are traveling elders sent by the Twelve to testify worldwide and prepare the way for the Lord.

f.w: prepare a way before my face

chapters.n: The difference: seventies travel continually; elders preside over local branches from time to time.
Vinson Knight, Samuel H. Smith, and Shadrach Roundy are to preside over the bishopric, as explained in the Doctrine and Covenants.

f.g: Joseph’s brother and one of the Eight Witnesses; he died in July 1844, weeks after the martyrdom.

f.w: the book of Doctrine and Covenants
f.g: The 1835 edition, which contained the revelation on priesthood (now D&C 107).

chapters.n: Presidents and counselors of priests, teachers, deacons, and the stake are also named or provided for.

f.g: Nauvoo presiding priest; he also helped build the temple.

chapters.n: These offices and keys are given to help govern, minister, and perfect the Saints.
The Saints must sustain or reject these names at general conference—the principle of common consent.

f.g: Common consent: members vote to sustain leaders.

chapters.n: Rooms should be prepared in the temple for these priesthood quorums.

f.w: prepare rooms for all these offices in my house
f.g: The Nauvoo Temple’s upper floors included offices and rooms for councils.

chapters.n: In March 1841 the question was asked: what does the Lord want for the Saints living across the Mississippi in Iowa Territory? Many had settled there after leaving Missouri.

f.g: Iowa became a U.S. territory in 1838 and a state in 1846; Saints settled around Montrose, across the river from Nauvoo.

chapters.n: Those trying to be Saints should gather to places Joseph designates and build cities to the Lord’s name, preparing for future events.

f.g: Trying, attempting.

f.w: build up cities unto my name

chapters.n: A city is to be built across the river from Nauvoo and named Zarahemla—after the great Nephite city in the Book of Mormon.
Saints from every direction may settle in Zarahemla, Nashville (also in Iowa), Nauvoo, or any appointed stake.

f.g: A small settlement in Lee County, Iowa, not the Tennessee city.
Settle and receive land as their portion.

chapters.n: Given July 9, 1841, at Brigham Young’s log home in Nauvoo, just after he returned from leading the Twelve’s mission to Britain. The Lord tenderly releases him from leaving his family as he had so often before—his sacrifice is accepted.

f.g: An unusually warm opening, written in Joseph Smith’s hand as he recorded the revelation.

f.w: your offering is acceptable to me

chapters.n: The Lord has seen all his labor and travels. Brigham had served many missions and had left his family sick and poor when he departed for England in 1839.

f.g: Travels, especially missionary journeys.

chapters.n: Brigham should now send the word abroad through others and take special care of his family from now on.

f.w: take especial care of your family

chapters.n: In August 1842 Missouri officials sought to extradite Joseph on false charges connected with an attempt on former governor Lilburn Boggs’s life. Joseph went into hiding and wrote this letter on September 1, explaining he had left his affairs in good hands and would return when the storm passed.

f.w: my enemies, both in Missouri and this State
f.g: Missouri sought Joseph’s arrest as an accessory in the 1842 shooting of Lilburn W. Boggs; Joseph was later freed by a federal judge in January 1843.
Of the worst kind.

chapters.n: Joseph reflects that envy and anger have followed him all his life—perhaps because he was foreordained for a purpose. “Deep water” is familiar to him; like Paul, he glories in trials because God has always delivered him.

f.w: deep water is what I am wont to swim in
f.g: Wont = accustomed. Trouble had become normal for him.

f.w: ordained from before the foundation of the world

chapters.n: The Saints should rejoice: Israel’s God is their God and will justly repay their oppressors.

f.g: Measure out, distribute.

chapters.n: The Lord commands that temple building continue without stopping, with redoubled diligence. Persecution is nothing new; the prophets endured it, and heaven holds a reward.

f.g: Doubled again; greatly increased.

chapters.n: Joseph now gives instructions about baptism for the dead.
Each baptism for the dead must have a recorder who personally sees and hears it, so he can testify truthfully. Witnesses and records make the ordinance valid.
What is properly recorded on earth will be recorded in heaven—the binding and loosing power Jesus gave Peter.

f.w: whatsoever you bind on earth, may be bound in heaven

chapters.n: The Lord is about to restore much more pertaining to the priesthood—fulfilled in the Nauvoo temple ordinances.
Records must be kept orderly and stored in the temple archives for future generations—a foundation of the Church’s family history work.

f.g: A place where important records are preserved.

chapters.n: Joseph had wanted to preach about baptism for the dead the next Sunday, but in hiding he will write the Lord’s word and send it by mail.

f.g: From the speaker’s platform at a public meeting.

chapters.n: He must close quickly; enemies are watching. Quoting Jesus, he says Satan “hath nothing in me”—no hold over him.

f.w: the prince of this world cometh, but he hath nothing in me

chapters.n: Joseph prays that all may be saved and signs as their servant and prophet.
Writing on September 6, 1842, while still in hiding, Joseph returns to baptism for the dead—the subject weighing most on his mind.

f.w: press itself upon my feelings the strongest
f.g: Joseph felt deep urgency about the salvation of the dead.

chapters.n: He recalls his earlier instruction that a recorder must witness each baptism with his own eyes and ears.

f.w: a recorder, who should be eye-witness

chapters.n: Since one recorder can’t attend everything, each ward of Nauvoo should have its own careful recorder, noting dates, names, and details, plus about three witnesses—following the biblical rule of two or three witnesses.

f.w: in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established

f.g: Avoid or remove (a difficulty).
In Nauvoo, a civic division of the city; the term later became the Church’s local congregation.

chapters.n: Ward records then go to a general Church recorder, who enters them in the general record with the certificates. Done properly, this is as valid as if he had witnessed them himself.

f.g: Shall fulfill the ordinance’s requirements.

chapters.n: This may seem detailed, but it follows an order God established before the world for saving those who died without the gospel.

f.w: die without a knowledge of the gospel

chapters.n: Joseph quotes John’s vision of the dead being judged from the books, including the book of life.
Joseph interprets: “the books” are earthly records of what was done; “the book of life” is heaven’s record. Earth’s records and heaven’s records correspond.
This ordinance depends on priesthood power to bind and loose. Put another way: what is recorded on earth is recorded in heaven. People are judged by ordinances done personally or by proxy.

f.g: Latin, “in one’s own person”—personally rather than by proxy.

f.w: by the means of their own agents
f.g: Through proxies who stand in for them.

chapters.n: This may sound bold, but whenever God gave a dispensation of priesthood, this power came with it. Ordinances done with authority and faithfully recorded become binding in heaven.

f.w: This is a faithful saying. Who can hear it?

chapters.n: As precedent, Joseph quotes Jesus giving Peter the keys of the kingdom and the power to bind and loose.
The key to it all—the “summum bonum”—is gaining the powers of the holy priesthood. With those keys, knowledge about saving the living and the dead follows.

f.g: Latin, “the highest good.”

chapters.n: Baptism by immersion represents death and resurrection: going down into the water like burial, coming up like rising from the grave. This symbolism ties naturally to baptism for the dead.

f.w: in the likeness of the resurrection

chapters.n: So the baptismal font represents the grave and is placed below where the living gather. Temple fonts are still located on a lower level, often resting on twelve oxen.

f.g: Similitude = likeness, symbol.

chapters.n: Quoting Paul: the natural comes first, then the spiritual. As earthly records are faithfully kept, so heaven’s records are kept. This is the sealing power and, in one sense, the “key of knowledge.”

f.w: The first man is of the earth, earthy

chapters.n: One of the great principles of family history: our ancestors’ salvation is necessary to ours. As Paul taught, they cannot be made perfect without us—nor we without them.

f.w: they without us cannot be made perfect

chapters.n: Joseph cites Paul’s mention of people being baptized for the dead as evidence the practice existed anciently.
He quotes Malachi’s prophecy of Elijah turning hearts of fathers and children toward each other, calling baptism for the dead “this most glorious of all subjects.”

f.w: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet

chapters.n: Joseph explains: there must be a “welding link” between generations—baptism for the dead and sealing. All dispensations, keys, and glories since Adam will be welded together, and hidden truths revealed to the humble.

f.g: A strong bond fusing two parts into one.

chapters.n: Joseph bursts into joy: the gospel is a voice of gladness, mercy, and truth for the living and the dead. He quotes Isaiah’s “how beautiful upon the mountains.”

f.w: a voice of truth out of the earth

f.g: Mount Carmel in Israel was known for heavy, refreshing dew and fertility.

chapters.n: He recounts the Restoration: Moroni at Cumorah, the Three Witnesses at Fayette, Michael exposing the devil on the Susquehanna, and Peter, James, and John restoring keys in the wilderness between Harmony and Colesville.

f.w: The voice of Peter, James, and John

chapters.n: God spoke in Peter Whitmer Sr.’s home in Fayette and in many places since. Angels—Michael (Adam), Gabriel, Raphael, and others—restored their keys “line upon line.”

f.w: the chamber of old Father Whitmer
f.g: The Church was organized in the Peter Whitmer Sr. home on April 6, 1830.
An angel named in Jewish tradition; his specific role in the Restoration is not otherwise explained.

f.w: line upon line, precept upon precept

chapters.n: A rousing call: go forward, not backward! Courage! Let even the dead praise Christ, who ordained a way to free them from their spirit prison.

f.g: Hebrew “God with us,” a title of Christ.

chapters.n: All creation is invited to rejoice—mountains, seas, rivers, trees, rocks, sun, moon, and stars—echoing the morning stars singing at creation.

f.g: Small streams.

chapters.n: Quoting Malachi on the Lord as a refiner, Joseph urges the Saints to offer an “offering in righteousness”: a book of their dead’s records presented in the finished temple.

f.w: like a refiner's fire, and like fuller's soap

f.g: A strong cleaning agent used to whiten cloth.

f.w: a book containing the records of our dead

chapters.n: Joseph closes warmly, promising more on the subject, as their humble servant and steadfast friend.

f.g: A friend who never turns aside or wavers.

chapters.n: On February 9, 1843, Joseph taught how to tell true messengers from false. First, angels can be resurrected beings with physical bodies of flesh and bones.
Jesus himself showed this after his resurrection, inviting disciples to touch him.
Second, “spirits of just men made perfect”—righteous people who have died but not yet been resurrected—who share the same glory.

f.w: spirits of just men made perfect

chapters.n: A practical test: if a messenger claims to come from God, offer to shake his hand.

f.g: A simple, physical test of the messenger’s nature.

chapters.n: A resurrected angel will shake hands, and you will feel it.
A righteous spirit without a body will appear in his glory, since that is the only way he can appear.

f.g: Surrounded by light.

chapters.n: He won’t shake hands, since that would be deceptive—implying he has a body. But he will still deliver his message.

f.w: contrary to the order of heaven for a just man to deceive
f.g: Honesty is part of heaven’s order; a righteous spirit won’t pretend.

chapters.n: If it is the devil pretending to be an angel of light, he will offer his hand, but you will feel nothing—exposing him.

f.w: the devil as an angel of light

chapters.n: These are three great “keys” to discern whether a heavenly visitation is from God.

f.g: A ministering visit or service.

chapters.n: These are teachings Joseph gave on April 2, 1843, at Ramus, Illinois. First: when Christ appears, we’ll see him as he truly is—a glorified man, like us in form.

f.w: we shall see him as he is

chapters.n: The friendships and social bonds we enjoy here will continue in heaven, but with eternal glory added.

f.g: Companionship, social relationships.

chapters.n: Joseph corrects a common belief: John 14:23 describes a real, personal visit of the Father and Son, not just a feeling in the heart.

f.g: Belonging to a sect or denomination; here, traditional Christian teaching of the time.

chapters.n: A question: is time measured differently for God, angels, prophets, and humans according to where they live?

f.g: Counting or calculation.

chapters.n: Yes. And only angels who belong or have belonged to this earth minister to it.

f.w: angels who minister to this earth

chapters.n: Angels don’t live on a planet like ours.

f.g: Live, dwell.

chapters.n: They live in God’s presence, on a globe like a sea of glass and fire, where past, present, and future are all visible.

f.w: a sea of glass and fire

chapters.n: God’s dwelling place is itself a great Urim and Thummim—a means of seeing and knowing all things.

f.g: Hebrew, often understood as “lights and perfections”; sacred instruments for receiving revelation.

chapters.n: The earth itself will become like crystal, a Urim and Thummim for its celestial inhabitants, revealing lower kingdoms. It will belong to Christ.

f.w: This earth, in its sanctified and immortal state

chapters.n: The “white stone” in Revelation 2:17 will become a personal Urim and Thummim for each who receives one, revealing higher kingdoms.

f.w: the white stone mentioned in Revelation 2:17

chapters.n: Each who enters the celestial kingdom receives a white stone with a new name only he knows—the “key word.”
Joseph prophesies that bloodshed before Christ’s coming will begin in South Carolina—fulfilled when the Civil War began there in 1861.
It would likely arise over slavery. Joseph says he received this on December 25, 1832—the same date as D&C 87.

f.g: The controversy over slavery, a central cause of the American Civil War.

chapters.n: Joseph once prayed earnestly to know when Christ would come, and heard a voice.

f.w: the time of the coming of the Son of Man

chapters.n: The voice: if Joseph lived to 85, he would see Christ’s face—so stop asking. Joseph would have turned 85 in December 1890.

f.w: let this suffice, and trouble me no more
f.g: Suffice = be enough. God sometimes withholds exact timing.

chapters.n: Joseph couldn’t tell whether this meant the Millennium, some earlier appearance, or seeing Christ after his own death. He honestly admits his uncertainty.

f.g: He was left with an ambiguous answer.

chapters.n: His conclusion: Christ will not come before that time.

f.w: will not be any sooner than that time

chapters.n: A beloved teaching: whatever intelligence we gain in this life rises with us in the resurrection. Learning has eternal value.

f.g: Light and truth; understanding.

chapters.n: Someone who gains more knowledge through diligence and obedience will have that advantage in the next life.

f.g: Both effort and righteous living are named; knowledge here is more than information.

chapters.n: There is an unchangeable law, decreed before the world, on which every blessing depends.

f.g: Unable to be reversed or cancelled.
Based or founded on.

chapters.n: When we receive any blessing, it is through obeying the law it depends on.
A defining doctrine: the Father and Son have tangible bodies of flesh and bones; the Holy Ghost is a spirit, which is why he can dwell within us.

f.w: The Father has a body of flesh and bones

chapters.n: A person may receive the Holy Ghost’s influence briefly without it remaining with him; keeping it requires worthiness.
Teaching at Ramus, Illinois, on May 16, 1843, Joseph explains that the celestial kingdom itself has three heavens or levels.
To reach the highest level, a man (and his wife) must enter the new and everlasting covenant of marriage—a priesthood order of eternal marriage.
Without it, the highest degree cannot be obtained.
He may enter another degree, but his kingdom ends there—he cannot have “increase,” meaning eternal family and posterity.

f.g: Eternal offspring and growth of family; “eternal lives.”

chapters.n: On May 17 Joseph explained Peter’s “more sure word of prophecy”: knowing by revelation that one is sealed up to eternal life through priesthood power.

f.w: The more sure word of prophecy

chapters.n: It is impossible to be saved in ignorance—especially ignorance of Jesus Christ and the saving truths of the gospel.
A distinctive teaching: there is no such thing as immaterial substance. Spirit is matter—just finer and purer, seen only by purified eyes.
We can’t see spirit now, but when our bodies are purified we will see that it is all matter.

This revelation was recorded July 12, 1843, in Nauvoo, though Joseph Smith had learned some of its principles years earlier while translating the Bible. It begins with his question: how were Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and Solomon justified in having multiple wives?

f.g: Joseph likely asked around 1831 while revising the Old Testament (JST); the revelation was written down in 1843 at Hyrum Smith’s request.
In the Old Testament, legal wives of secondary status, not illicit partners.

chapters.n: The Lord promises to answer the question.

f.g: Concerning.

chapters.n: Joseph must prepare his heart to receive and obey. Those to whom a law is revealed are accountable for it.

The Lord reveals a “new and everlasting covenant.” Rejecting it keeps one from God’s highest glory. In this section the phrase refers especially to eternal marriage, which is part of the fulness of the gospel covenant.

f.w: a new and an everlasting covenant

f.g: Stopped in progress; unable to receive the fullest blessings.

chapters.n: Every blessing comes by obeying the law God appointed for it before the world was made.

f.w: abide the law which was appointed for that blessing

chapters.n: The new and everlasting covenant is designed for the fulness of God’s glory; receiving that fulness requires keeping its law.

A key verse: any covenant or relationship not sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise—through the one holding sealing keys—ends at death. Only one person at a time holds these keys on earth; today it is the President of the Church.

f.g: The Holy Ghost’s role in ratifying ordinances as valid in eternity, based on faithfulness.

f.w: there is never but one on the earth at a time
f.g: The President of the Church holds and directs all sealing keys.
Power to produce an effect.

chapters.n: God’s house is orderly, not confused.
Will God accept an offering not made in his name? The rhetorical question expects “no.”
Or receive something he hasn’t authorized?

f.w: that which I have not appointed

chapters.n: God appoints blessings only by law, as he and the Father ordained before the world.
No one comes to the Father except through Christ and his word—his law.

f.w: no man shall come unto the Father but by me

chapters.n: Everything not established by God—even human institutions and honors—will fall and not survive death or resurrection.
What God establishes endures; what he doesn’t will be shaken and destroyed.
So a marriage made only “until death” and not by God’s authority ends at death.

f.w: so long as he is in the world
f.g: Compare the common vow “till death do us part.”

chapters.n: After death such people neither marry nor are given in marriage—Jesus’ words—and serve as ministering angels to those who receive greater glory.

f.w: they neither marry nor are given in marriage

chapters.n: Not having kept this law, they remain single and separate, saved but not exalted—angels rather than gods.

f.g: Cannot grow into eternal family and increase.

chapters.n: Even a marriage meant to be eternal is not valid after death unless performed by God’s authority and sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise. Heaven’s gatekeepers will not let it pass.

f.w: the angels and the gods are appointed there
f.g: Sentinels who admit only those properly sealed.

chapters.n: But a marriage done by God’s law, sealed by proper authority, and kept faithfully will endure: the couple will come forth in the resurrection and inherit thrones and kingdoms, with “a continuation of the seeds”—eternal posterity.

f.g: Eternal increase; the power to have posterity forever.

chapters.n: Such couples become gods—without end, above all, with all power. Latter-day Saints understand this as exaltation through Christ, always worshipping the Father and Son.
This glory cannot be reached without keeping this law.
Echoing Jesus: the gate is narrow, and few find the way to exaltation, because they don’t receive or know Christ.

f.w: strait is the gate, and narrow the way

f.g: Narrow, tight.

chapters.n: Receiving Christ in this life leads to truly knowing him and to exaltation—being where he is.

f.w: where I am ye shall be also

chapters.n: “Eternal lives” is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ. The plural suggests the eternal family continuing.
The broad road leads to “the deaths”—the end of increase—because people do not receive Christ or his law.

f.w: Broad is the gate, and wide the way

chapters.n: A difficult verse: sealed persons who later sin seriously (short of murder) may still be exalted, but only after severe suffering—“destroyed in the flesh” and given to “the buffetings of Satan.” Church leaders have stressed that this is no license to sin and that repentance is still required.

f.g: Being left to Satan’s afflictions as a consequence of sin.

chapters.n: Blasphemy against the Holy Ghost—the unpardonable sin—includes shedding innocent blood and consenting to Christ’s death after having received this covenant.

f.w: The blasphemy against the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: The Lord will give Joseph the law of the priesthood ordained before the world.

f.w: the law of my Holy Priesthood
f.g: Here especially the laws governing sealing and eternal marriage.

chapters.n: Abraham received everything by revelation and is now exalted on his throne.
God promised Abraham descendants as countless as stars and sand—in this world and beyond. Joseph is among his seed.
The promise belongs to Joseph too, as Abraham’s seed. This law continues the Father’s work, by which he is glorified.
“Do the works of Abraham”—enter God’s law and be saved.
Those who don’t cannot receive the promise made to Abraham.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham as a wife, and from Hagar came many people (through Ishmael). The revelation presents this as part of fulfilling God’s promises.

f.w: Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham to wife

chapters.n: Was Abraham condemned? No, because God commanded it.

f.w: Verily I say unto you, Nay

chapters.n: Abraham was also commanded to offer Isaac, despite the command “Thou shalt not kill.” His obedience was counted as righteousness. God’s specific commands define what is right.

f.w: Abraham was commanded to offer his son Isaac
it was accounted unto him for righteousness

chapters.n: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did only what they were commanded and are now exalted—gods, not angels.

f.w: they have entered into their exaltation

chapters.n: David, Solomon, Moses, and others had plural wives. They sinned only where they acted without God’s authorization.

f.w: save in those things which they received not of me

chapters.n: David’s wives were given through Nathan and other prophets; his only sin in this was with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah, for which he lost his exaltation.

f.w: in the case of Uriah and his wife

chapters.n: The Lord reminds Joseph he is appointed to restore all things.
Joseph had asked about adultery. A wife in this covenant who is with another man without divine authorization commits adultery.

f.g: Divine authorization through the sealing power.

chapters.n: A woman outside the covenant who is with another man also commits adultery. The moral law applies to all.
A husband under covenant who is with another woman breaks his vow and commits adultery. The standard applies to husbands too.
If a wife is innocent and the husband guilty, Joseph has authority by revelation to seal her to a faithful man.
Joseph holds the keys through which all things are restored.

f.w: the keys and power of the priesthood

chapters.n: The sealing power: what Joseph seals or binds on earth by God’s word is bound in heaven. Even remitting or retaining sins is included.

f.w: whatsoever you seal on earth shall be sealed in heaven

chapters.n: Those Joseph blesses, the Lord will bless—a promise also given to Abraham.

f.w: whomsoever you bless I will bless

chapters.n: Whatever Joseph does by God’s word and law will be blessed and without condemnation.
The Lord seals Joseph’s exaltation and prepares a throne for him with Abraham.

f.w: I seal upon you your exaltation

chapters.n: The Lord has seen Joseph’s sacrifices and forgives his sins, offering escape—as with Abraham, who was stopped from sacrificing Isaac.

f.w: as I accepted the offering of Abraham

chapters.n: Emma Smith is addressed. The meaning of this verse is uncertain; it seems to refer to some offer or test that the Lord now withdraws, “to prove you all,” as Abraham was tested.

f.g: Prove = test.

chapters.n: Emma is asked to accept the virtuous women sealed to Joseph. Historians note that this was extremely painful for Emma, who struggled with and at times opposed plural marriage.

f.w: receive all those that have been given unto my servant Joseph
f.g: Joseph was sealed to a number of women in Nauvoo; the details remain incompletely documented.

chapters.n: Joseph has been faithful in a few things and will be made ruler over many and strengthened.
Emma is commanded to stay with Joseph and no one else, with a severe warning if she does not abide God’s law.

f.g: Hold fast to; be faithful to.

chapters.n: If Emma doesn’t accept it, Joseph will still keep his promises to her, and the Lord will bless him a hundredfold—echoing Jesus’ promise to those who sacrifice.
Emma should forgive Joseph’s trespasses, and she will be forgiven and blessed with joy. Forgiveness in marriage runs both ways.

f.w: forgive my servant Joseph his trespasses

chapters.n: Joseph should not give away his property, lest enemies destroy him. Some suggest this relates to financial arrangements protecting Emma and the family.

f.w: put his property out of his hands
f.g: Transfer ownership of his property.

chapters.n: Now the Lord turns to more of the law of the priesthood.

f.w: there are many things pertaining thereunto
f.g: Indicates the revelation is only partial.

chapters.n: A man called of God as Aaron was, who acts by God’s word and keys, does not sin and will be justified.

f.w: called of my Father, as was Aaron

chapters.n: No one should attack Joseph; the Lord will justify him, and Joseph will offer the sacrifice required for his own transgressions.

f.g: Attack or oppose.

chapters.n: This verse describes plural marriage as practiced under divine authorization at that time, including the first wife’s consent. The Church discontinued plural marriage through the 1890 Manifesto; today only monogamous marriages are performed and anyone practicing polygamy cannot remain a member.

f.g: Marry, take as a spouse.

chapters.n: The revelation states that wives given by this law do not make the husband an adulterer, because they are lawfully his.

f.g: A number used for illustration, not a quota.

chapters.n: Such wives are given to “multiply and replenish the earth” and bear the souls of men, continuing the Father’s work. The verse states the stated purpose of the practice in that era.

f.g: Bring spirit children of God into mortal life.

chapters.n: If a wife taught this law rejects it, the verse warns of destruction. Historians and Church leaders acknowledge this teaching placed great strain on Emma and other women.

f.g: Support, assist.

chapters.n: If she does not receive the law, the husband may still receive what God gives him and is exempt from the “law of Sarah”—the pattern of a first wife consenting, as Sarah gave Hagar.
More will be revealed later. The Lord, Alpha and Omega, closes for now. Latter-day Saints today emphasize this section’s enduring teaching on eternal marriage and families.

f.w: I will reveal more unto you, hereafter

chapters.n: Given November 3, 1831, at Hiram, Ohio, this revelation was called “the Appendix” to the planned Book of Commandments, just as section 1 was its preface. The Lord calls his Church to listen.

f.w: Hearken, O ye people of my church

chapters.n: The Lord will come suddenly to his temple and bring judgment on nations and individuals who forget God—even within the Church.
He will “make bare his holy arm”—roll up his sleeve and act openly—and the whole earth will see his salvation.
“Prepare ye, prepare ye.” The Saints are to become holy and gather to Zion, except those told to stay where they are.

f.g: Remain.

chapters.n: “Go ye out from Babylon”—leave the world’s wickedness. Those who carry holy things must be clean, as the priests who carried temple vessels were.

f.w: Be ye clean that bear the vessels of the Lord

f.g: In scripture, a symbol of worldliness and spiritual corruption.

chapters.n: Hold sacred gatherings, speak often to one another about spiritual things, and pray.
The call is repeated: leave Babylon and gather from all directions.
Elders are to go to distant nations and islands—first to the Gentiles, then to the Jews, reversing the order of Jesus’ day.

f.w: first upon the Gentiles, and then upon the Jews

chapters.n: Their message: come to Zion so its borders grow, its stakes are strengthened, and it spreads outward.
Using Jesus’ parable of the ten virgins, the cry goes out: wake up and go meet the Bridegroom—Christ.
Be watchful; no one knows the exact time.

f.w: ye know neither the day nor the hour

chapters.n: Those among the Gentiles should flee spiritually and physically to Zion.
Those of Judah should flee to Jerusalem and its temple mount. Two great gathering centers are envisioned.

f.w: the mountains of the Lord's house

chapters.n: Babylon is spiritual wickedness, not just a place.
Don’t flee in panic; prepare first. And don’t look back with longing—as Lot’s wife did.

f.w: let not your flight be in haste

chapters.n: All people everywhere are commanded to repent.

f.w: commandeth all men everywhere to repent

chapters.n: An angel cries through heaven, “Prepare ye the way of the Lord”—the message of John the Baptist, now for the Second Coming.

f.w: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, and make his paths straight

chapters.n: Christ the Lamb will stand on Mount Zion with 144,000 bearing the Father’s name on their foreheads.
So prepare and go out to meet the Bridegroom.

f.w: go ye out to meet him

chapters.n: He will stand on the Mount of Olives, the ocean, the islands, and Zion—his presence will reach everywhere.
His voice will go out from both Zion and Jerusalem and be heard by all.

f.w: utter his voice out of Zion

chapters.n: His voice will be like rushing waters and thunder, leveling mountains and filling valleys.
The great ocean will be driven north and the islands joined into one land—a restoration of the earth’s ancient condition.

f.w: the islands shall become one land

chapters.n: Jerusalem and Zion will return to their original places, and the earth will be as it was before it was divided in Peleg’s day.
Christ the Savior will stand among his people and reign over all.
Those in the “north countries”—understood as the lost ten tribes—will be remembered. Their prophets will act, rocks will be struck, and ice will melt before them.

f.w: they who are in the north countries

chapters.n: A highway will be raised up in the midst of the deep for their return.

f.w: an highway shall be cast up

chapters.n: Their enemies will no longer threaten them.

f.g: Fall into their power.

chapters.n: Deserts will gush with living water; dry land will thirst no more.
They will bring their treasures to the children of Ephraim, who hold the birthright and priesthood responsibility to bless Israel.
Even the ancient hills will tremble at their coming.
In Zion they will bow and be crowned with glory by Ephraim’s descendants—understood as receiving temple blessings.
They will be filled with songs of everlasting joy.
This is God’s blessing on all Israel, with the “richer blessing” on Ephraim and his companions.

f.w: the richer blessing upon the head of Ephraim

chapters.n: Judah too, after long suffering, will be made holy and dwell in God’s presence forever.
An angel flying through heaven with the everlasting gospel has appeared to some—understood by Latter-day Saints as Moroni and other restoring messengers.

f.w: mine angel flying through the midst of heaven

chapters.n: This gospel will be preached to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people.

f.w: every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people

chapters.n: Messengers will cry loudly: Fear God and glorify him, for judgment has come.

f.w: Fear God and give glory to him

chapters.n: Worship the Creator of heaven, earth, sea, and springs.
The faithful pray day and night, quoting Isaiah: “O that thou wouldst rend the heavens and come down!”

f.w: O that thou wouldst rend the heavens

f.g: Tear open.

chapters.n: The prayer will be answered: the Lord’s presence will be like fire that melts and makes water boil.

f.w: the fire which causeth the waters to boil

chapters.n: He will come to make his name known to his enemies, and nations will tremble.

f.w: make thy name known to thine adversaries

chapters.n: He does awesome, unexpected things.

f.w: terrible things, things they look not for

f.g: Awe-inspiring.

chapters.n: When he comes, he will meet those who joyfully do right and remember him.

f.w: him who rejoiceth and worketh righteousness

chapters.n: No ear has heard or eye seen the great things God prepares for those who wait for him.
Quoting Isaiah 63, people ask: who is this coming from heaven in dyed garments, glorious and strong?
He answers: I am the righteous one, mighty to save.
He will wear red, like someone who has trampled grapes in a winepress. The red recalls both judgment and his atoning blood.

f.g: A pit where grapes were trodden underfoot to press out juice.

chapters.n: His glory will outshine the sun, darken the moon, and hurl stars from their places.

f.w: the sun shall hide his face in shame

chapters.n: “I have trodden the winepress alone”—Christ bore the full weight both of the Atonement and of judgment by himself.

f.w: I have trodden the wine-press alone

chapters.n: The vivid image of stained garments describes the day of vengeance on persistent wickedness.
Now “the year of my redeemed” has come; they will speak forever of the Lord’s loving kindness.
A tender verse: in all their afflictions he was afflicted. In love and pity he redeemed and carried them all along.

f.w: In all their afflictions he was afflicted

f.g: Possibly the Lord himself or his messenger; the Hebrew is debated.

chapters.n: Enoch, Noah, Moses, and the prophets before them are included among the redeemed.

f.w: Enoch also, and they who were with him

chapters.n: From Moses to Elijah to John the Baptist, the apostles, and the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—all will stand before the Lamb.

f.w: who were with Christ in his resurrection

chapters.n: The graves of the Saints will open, and they will stand at Christ’s right hand on Mount Zion and the New Jerusalem, singing the song of the Lamb forever.

f.w: the graves of the saints shall be opened

chapters.n: For this purpose the Lord sent the fulness of his gospel, explained plainly and simply.
It prepares the weak for coming events, when the weak will confound the wise and a small people will become strong.

f.w: the little one become a strong nation
two shall put their tens of thousands to flight

chapters.n: Through humble people and the Spirit, the Lord will “thresh the nations”—separate wheat from chaff.
These revelations were first kept from the world but are now to be published to all.

f.w: commanded to be kept from the world
f.g: Early revelations circulated privately before the Book of Commandments was printed.

chapters.n: This is the will of the Lord, who rules all.
Those who repent and become holy will receive eternal life.
Those who will not listen will be “cut off,” as Moses prophesied of those who reject the prophet like unto him.

f.w: cut off from among the people

chapters.n: Malachi’s prophecy of a day burning like an oven, leaving the proud neither root nor branch.
Here is the Lord’s answer to them.

f.g: What follows largely echoes Isaiah 50.

chapters.n: When he came to his own, they did not receive him.
When he called, no one answered—yet his arm was never too short to save.
At his rebuke, seas dry and rivers become desert—echoing the Exodus.
He can darken the heavens as if dressed in mourning sackcloth.

f.g: Coarse dark cloth worn in mourning.

chapters.n: Those who reject him will lie down in sorrow.

f.w: ye shall lie down in sorrow

chapters.n: No one can deliver them, because they rejected the Lord’s voice and his servants.
The servants sealed up their testimony, and the rejecters were left in darkness.

f.w: sealed up the testimony and bound up the law

chapters.n: They go to outer darkness, with weeping and gnashing of teeth.
The Lord God has spoken. The appendix closes as firmly as the preface opened.

f.w: the Lord your God hath spoken it

chapters.n: This declaration was adopted by a Church general assembly in Kirtland on August 17, 1835, and included in the first edition of the Doctrine and Covenants. It is a statement of belief, not a revelation. It begins: governments are ordained by God for people’s good, and God holds lawmakers and officials accountable.

f.g: The section was likely written by Oliver Cowdery while Joseph Smith was away; it reflects the Church’s official position.

chapters.n: Peaceful government must protect three things: freedom of conscience, the right to own and control property, and the protection of life.

f.g: Kept unbroken; never violated.

chapters.n: Governments need officials to enforce laws. People should seek out and support fair, just officials—by vote in a republic or by the ruler’s choice in a monarchy.

f.g: Civil officers such as judges.
Fairness.

chapters.n: Religion comes from God, and people answer to God alone for how they worship—unless their practices infringe on others’ rights. Government should restrain crime but never control conscience.

f.g: Answerable, accountable.

f.w: should restrain crime, but never control conscience

chapters.n: Citizens should support the governments that protect their rights; rebellion against such governments is wrong. Governments may make laws for the public good while respecting freedom of conscience.

f.g: Speech or action inciting rebellion against the government.
Unable to be taken away or given up.

chapters.n: Leaders deserve honor for protecting the innocent and punishing the guilty. Without laws, anarchy follows. Human laws govern relations among people; divine laws govern faith and worship. We answer to God for both.

f.g: Respectful submission.
Replaced, overthrown.

chapters.n: Governments must protect religious freedom and have no right to punish people for their beliefs, provided they respect the law and do not promote rebellion.

f.g: Forbid, condemn, or outlaw.

chapters.n: Crimes should be punished according to their seriousness by the laws where they occur, and all citizens should help bring lawbreakers to justice.

f.g: Peace and calm.

chapters.n: Religion and civil government should not be mixed so that one church is favored and another oppressed.

f.w: mingle religious influence with civil government
f.g: The Saints had felt the effects of religious hostility in Missouri.

chapters.n: Churches may discipline their own members regarding fellowship, but may not seize property, threaten life, or inflict physical punishment. The most a church can do is excommunicate.

f.g: Remove from membership.
Danger.

chapters.n: Wrongs should be taken to the courts. But people may defend themselves, their friends, property, and government from unlawful attack in an emergency when the law can’t help in time.

f.g: Remedy or compensation for a wrong.
Urgent need; emergency.

chapters.n: Written in 1835 after Missourians accused the Saints of stirring up enslaved people, this verse states the Church would not preach to or baptize enslaved people against their masters’ will. It reflects that era’s legal and political pressures. Later scripture and teaching affirm that God invites all to come unto him, “black and white, bond and free.”

f.g: Enslaved people.

chapters.n: Written by John Taylor, an eyewitness, this section announces the martyrdom of Joseph Smith and his brother Hyrum on June 27, 1844, at Carthage Jail, Illinois. A mob of 150–200 men with blackened faces attacked; both brothers were killed.

f.g: The attackers darkened their faces with mud and gunpowder to hide their identities.
Joseph’s final words as he fell from the window.

chapters.n: John Taylor and Willard Richards were also in the room. Taylor was badly wounded; Richards escaped virtually unharmed, fulfilling an earlier prophecy by Joseph.

f.w: without even a hole in his robe
f.g: Joseph had reportedly prophesied that Willard Richards would escape unharmed.

chapters.n: John Taylor testifies that, apart from Jesus, Joseph did more for human salvation than anyone else. In about twenty years he brought forth the Book of Mormon, sent the gospel worldwide, received the revelations, gathered thousands, and founded Nauvoo. He and Hyrum were united in life and in death.

f.w: translated by the gift and power of God
In life they were not divided, and in death they were not separated

chapters.n: After being driven from Nauvoo in 1846, the Saints wintered at Winter Quarters (near today’s Omaha, Nebraska). On January 14, 1847, Brigham Young received this revelation for the “Camp of Israel”—a deliberate echo of ancient Israel in the wilderness.
Everyone—members and those traveling with them—should be organized into companies and covenant to keep God’s commandments.
Companies have captains over hundreds, fifties, and tens, each led by a president and two counselors under the Twelve—a pattern from Moses.

President Joseph F. Smith, sixth President of the Church and nephew of Joseph Smith, received this vision on October 3, 1918, about six weeks before his death. That year he had lost his son Hyrum Mack Smith, and the world was suffering from World War I and the influenza pandemic. He begins quietly, pondering scripture in his room.
He was reflecting on Christ’s atoning sacrifice for the redemption of the world.
He marveled at the love shown by both the Father and the Son in sending the Redeemer.
Through Christ’s Atonement and obedience to gospel principles, all humankind can be saved.
